days.title: Logging Design: Log Analytics Workspaces, Diagnostic Settings, Log Routing and Data Collection Rules

concepts.heading: How Many Workspaces?
concepts.body: Microsoft's workspace design guidance says to start with a single Log Analytics workspace and add another only when a concrete criterion demands it. Volume alone is never a reason: one large workspace performs fine and is easier to query across teams. Valid reasons are data residency (a workspace lives in one region), different retention for the same table on different resources, separate Microsoft Entra tenants, split billing or data ownership, and keeping Microsoft Sentinel data apart, because enabling Sentinel puts all data in that workspace under Sentinel pricing. Per-team visibility is not a reason: the default access control mode, Use resource or workspace permissions, lets a team with Reader on its resources query only those resources' rows in resource-context. Service providers keep a workspace per customer tenant and reach them with Azure Lighthouse. Many same-region workspaces that need customer-managed keys or a shared commitment discount can be linked to a dedicated cluster.

concepts.heading: Diagnostic Settings and Their Destinations
concepts.body: Platform metrics are collected automatically, but resource logs are not: a diagnostic setting on each resource decides which log categories (or category groups such as allLogs or audit) go where. A setting can send to a Log Analytics workspace for KQL queries and log alerts, to a Storage account for cheap long-term archive, to Event Hubs for streaming to a non-Microsoft SIEM, and to certain partner solutions, with each destination type at most once per setting. For regional resources the storage account and event hub must be in the same region as the resource. Data in a workspace cannot be edited but can be purged, so a tamper-proof archive belongs in storage with an immutability policy. The activity log, which records who created or deleted what, keeps events for only 90 days; a subscription-level diagnostic setting sends it to a workspace or storage to keep it longer. At scale, Azure Policy deploys diagnostic settings so new resources are covered automatically.

concepts.heading: Data Collection Rules and Azure Monitor Agent
concepts.body: Guest operating system data, such as Windows events, syslog, performance counters and text logs, is collected by Azure Monitor Agent, which replaced the legacy Log Analytics agent. The agent does nothing until a data collection rule (DCR) is associated with the machine. A DCR names the sources, an optional transformation and the destinations, and one DCR can be associated with hundreds of machines, so it acts as a central collection policy: change it once and every machine follows. Machines can have several DCRs, for example a baseline security rule and an application rule. Servers on-premises or in other clouds are first onboarded with Azure Arc, after which the same agent and DCRs work on them exactly as on Azure VMs. Custom applications send JSON through the Logs Ingestion API, which also names a DCR; the older HTTP Data Collector API is deprecated and does not work through an Azure Monitor Private Link Scope.

concepts.heading: Transformations, Table Plans and Retention
concepts.body: A transformation is a KQL statement inside a DCR that runs in the ingestion pipeline before data is stored. It can drop rows nobody needs, remove or mask a sensitive column so it never reaches the workspace, or parse text into columns. Data that arrives through diagnostic settings uses a workspace transformation DCR instead, for tables that support it. Each table then has a plan: Analytics for alerting and everyday queries, Basic for troubleshooting data with cheaper ingestion, a fixed 30 days of interactive queries and a charge per query, and Auxiliary for verbose data kept cheaply for a long time. Retention has two parts: analytics retention for interactive use, up to two years, and total retention up to 12 years, with older data reached through search jobs that copy matching rows into a new table. Because 31 days of retention are included in ingestion, cutting retention below that saves nothing; the real cost lever is ingesting less.

concepts.heading: Moving Data Out and Locking It Down
concepts.body: Several patterns move log data onward, and each fits a different need. Data export rules continuously copy selected workspace tables to storage or Event Hubs in the workspace's region as data arrives, unfiltered. Adding a destination to an existing diagnostic setting is lower latency when the source already uses one. Scheduled queries in Logic Apps or Functions can filter and aggregate, but they are bound by query limits and are not meant for large volumes. Summary rules aggregate detailed data on a schedule into a smaller table in the same workspace. For private connectivity, Azure Monitor uses an Azure Monitor Private Link Scope (AMPLS) rather than one private endpoint per resource. Because some endpoints are shared, Learn recommends one AMPLS for all networks that share a DNS. Its Private Only access mode lets clients reach only the workspaces listed in the scope, which is how a design prevents data exfiltration to other workspaces.

examPoints: A question listing several teams, regions or tenants is testing workspace criteria: add a workspace only for residency, tenant, retention, ownership, billing or Sentinel cost reasons, and solve per-team visibility with resource-context access.

A question about routing resource logs is testing diagnostic settings: a workspace for KQL and alerts, Event Hubs for an external SIEM, storage with immutability for cheap tamper-proof archive, and a setting on the subscription for the activity log beyond 90 days.
A question about keeping sensitive or useless data out of a workspace, or about cost, is testing DCR transformations and table plans, not access control or shorter retention.

quiz.q: A multinational keeps one Log Analytics workspace in East US. A new regulation says logs from resources in its German subsidiary must be stored in Germany, and the security team still wants one place to correlate data for the rest of the company. What should you recommend?
choices: Keep the single workspace and add table-level RBAC so that only German staff can read the rows produced by the German subsidiary
Keep the single workspace and set a longer retention period on the tables that receive data from the German subsidiary's resources
Add a workspace in a German region for the subsidiary's resources and keep the East US workspace for the rest of the company
Create one workspace per subsidiary worldwide so that each country has its own region, retention and access boundaries in place
quiz.explain: Each workspace lives in one region, so a residency rule is one of the few criteria that justifies a second workspace, and only for the data it covers. Choice A is tempting because access control is the usual answer for team boundaries, but permissions do not change where the data is stored.

quiz.q: Storage accounts send blob resource logs to a workspace through diagnostic settings. Reads by a backup tool make up most of the StorageRead volume and are never queried, but reads by other clients must be kept for investigations. The StorageBlobLogs table supports workspace transformations. How should you cut ingestion?
choices: Add a workspace transformation DCR that filters out the backup tool's read rows before they are stored in the workspace table
Clear the StorageRead category in the diagnostic setting so that no read operation by any client reaches the workspace
Lower the analytics retention of the storage tables to seven days so that the unwanted read rows are deleted from the workspace sooner
Create a data export rule for the storage tables so that the read rows are sent to an event hub instead of the workspace table
quiz.explain: Diagnostic settings select whole categories, so clearing StorageRead would also drop the reads that must be kept; a workspace transformation DCR on StorageBlobLogs drops only the backup tool's rows before ingestion. Choice C sounds like a saving, but ingestion is what is billed and retention below 31 days is already included.

days.recap: Start with one workspace and add more only for residency, tenant, retention, ownership or Sentinel reasons; route resource logs with diagnostic settings, collect guest data with Azure Monitor Agent and DCRs, and cut cost by ingesting less through transformations and the right table plan.

days.title: Monitoring Design: Alerts, Insights, Application Insights and Network Watcher

concepts.heading: Choosing the Alert Type
concepts.body: Azure Monitor has three main alert rule types, and the design choice is about what is measured and how wide one rule reaches. Metric alerts evaluate platform or custom metrics with low latency; one rule can cover many resources of the same type in the same region, and dynamic thresholds learn the metric's normal pattern, including daily and weekly seasonality, so you do not have to guess a static number. Log search alerts run a KQL query on a schedule against a workspace, so one rule covers every resource that sends data there, from any subscription or region, and splitting by the _ResourceId column produces one alert per resource. Activity log alerts react to control-plane events, such as someone deleting a resource, and also carry Service Health and Resource Health events. Pick metrics for fast, simple thresholds, log search for correlations and cross-region scope, and activity log alerts for management operations.

concepts.heading: Action Groups and Alert Processing Rules
concepts.body: An alert rule says when something is wrong; an action group says who or what is told. One action group can send email, SMS, push and voice notifications, open an ITSM ticket, and call automation such as an Azure Function, a Logic App, an Automation runbook, a webhook or Event Hubs. Reusing a few shared action groups across many rules keeps contact lists consistent. Alert processing rules change alerts as they fire without editing the rules. They can suppress action groups during a planned window, such as weekend patching, while the alerts are still recorded, or add an action group to every alert in a scope, such as sending all Sev0 alerts in production to the on-call team. Because they apply by scope and filter, they also cover alert rules created later. A design that copies the same notification settings into hundreds of rules is usually better served by these two building blocks.

concepts.heading: Insights and Health Views
concepts.body: Insights are curated monitoring experiences for one kind of resource. VM insights shows guest performance across machines, Container insights covers AKS nodes, pods and container logs, and other insights exist for storage, networks and Key Vault. They are built on workspaces, metrics and workbooks, so their data can also be queried and alerted on. Separate from your own telemetry is information from Microsoft about the platform. Azure status is the public page for widespread incidents. Service Health is the personalized view of service issues, planned maintenance and health advisories for the services and regions you actually use, and Service Health alerts send them through action groups. Resource Health tells you whether one specific resource, such as a single VM or database, is available now and whether a platform event caused a past outage. Use Service Health when Microsoft is telling you something about a service, and Resource Health when you ask about one resource.

concepts.heading: Application Insights
concepts.body: Application Insights is the application performance monitoring feature of Azure Monitor. It collects requests, dependencies, exceptions and traces from the code itself and correlates them across services, so you get an application map, end-to-end transaction views and failure and performance analysis. Microsoft recommends instrumenting with OpenTelemetry through the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro, a vendor-neutral approach, and each resource is workspace-based, storing its data in a Log Analytics workspace next to infrastructure logs. Availability monitoring probes a public endpoint from several Azure locations on a schedule; the Standard test is the current choice and can also check TLS certificate validity and warn before expiry, while URL ping tests are deprecated. Infrastructure tools such as Container insights or Network Watcher show nodes, pods and network paths, but they cannot tell you which request called which service or why it failed. That gap is what Application Insights fills.

concepts.heading: Network Watcher for Design and Troubleshooting
concepts.body: Network Watcher is a regional set of network monitoring and diagnostic tools. For ongoing visibility, virtual network flow logs record every IP flow in a virtual network, including whether network security rules allowed or denied it, and traffic analytics enriches them into maps and dashboards in a workspace. NSG flow logs are retiring and no longer accept new deployments, so new designs use virtual network flow logs. Connection monitor continuously measures reachability, latency and packet loss between Azure VMs, Arc-enabled on-premises hosts and endpoints such as URLs, with alerts when they degrade. For point-in-time diagnosis, next hop shows which route and next hop type a packet from a VM will use, IP flow verify shows whether a security rule allows or denies a packet and which rule decided, connection troubleshoot runs a one-time check, packet capture records traffic on a VM, and VPN troubleshoot diagnoses gateways. Exam answers pair each question with exactly one of these tools.

examPoints: A question about one rule covering many resources across regions, or one alert per resource, is testing log search alerts with splitting; a fast threshold on a single metric type in one region is a metric alert.
A question about silencing or redirecting notifications without editing rules is testing alert processing rules, and one about who gets told and what automation runs is testing action groups.

A question that asks for end-to-end request tracing points to Application Insights, outage and maintenance notices to Service Health, a single resource's state to Resource Health, and network paths to the matching Network Watcher tool.

quiz.q: An e-commerce API has a CPU metric that is high every weekday at noon and low at night. Static thresholds either fire every lunchtime or miss real problems at night. Operations wants one alert rule that adapts to the normal daily pattern. What should you recommend?
choices: A log search alert that runs every minute and compares CPU with a fixed value that is stored in a watchlist for each hour
A metric alert rule with dynamic thresholds, which learns the metric's history and seasonal patterns to set the boundaries
An activity log alert on the API resource that fires whenever its CPU metric changes more than expected by the operations team
An alert processing rule that suppresses notifications at noon every weekday so that the expected lunchtime peaks are ignored
quiz.explain: Dynamic thresholds use historical data to learn hourly, daily and weekly patterns and calculate boundaries, so one rule adapts to the noon peak. Choice D is tempting because it removes the noise, but it would also hide a real problem at noon and does nothing for the missed problems at night.

quiz.q: Every critical alert in a subscription must open an ITSM ticket and start an Azure Automation runbook that collects diagnostics. Alert rules are created by many teams, and the requirement must also cover rules added later without anyone editing them. What should you recommend?
choices: Ask each team to add its own email and SMS notifications to every alert rule, and to repeat this for each new rule it creates
Create an activity log alert on the subscription that fires whenever an alert rule is created and sends its details to the ITSM tool
Configure a Service Health alert for the subscription with an action group that opens tickets and starts the diagnostics runbook
Create an action group with ITSM and runbook actions, and an alert processing rule that adds it to critical alerts in the subscription
quiz.explain: An action group holds the ITSM and runbook actions once, and an alert processing rule scoped to the subscription and filtered by severity adds it to every matching alert, including those from future rules. Choice C is tempting because it also uses an action group, but Service Health alerts only carry Microsoft's service notices, not your own alert rules.

days.recap: Choose metric, log search or activity log alerts by data and scope, attach shared action groups and use alert processing rules for windows and scope-wide routing, and use Application Insights for request tracing, Service Health and Resource Health for platform status, and Network Watcher tools for network paths.

days.title: Authentication Design: Microsoft Entra ID, MFA, Conditional Access, Passwordless, External ID and Hybrid Identity

concepts.heading: Hybrid Sign-in: PHS, PTA or Federation
concepts.body: When users come from on-premises Active Directory, the design first decides where passwords are checked. Password hash synchronization (PHS) syncs a hash of the password hash, and Microsoft Entra ID validates sign-ins in the cloud; it needs the least infrastructure, keeps working if the datacenter is down, and is required for the leaked credentials report in Microsoft Entra ID Protection. Pass-through Authentication (PTA) uses lightweight on-premises agents that check each password against domain controllers, so lockouts, disabled accounts and logon hours apply at the moment of sign-in; Learn recommends three agents and PHS enabled as a manual backup. Federation, for example with AD FS, redirects sign-in to an on-premises identity provider and is chosen only for requirements the cloud methods cannot meet, such as a third-party sign-in method that depends on federation. Learn recommends enabling PHS in every design, even as a backup.

concepts.heading: Microsoft Entra Connect Sync or Cloud Sync
concepts.body: Synchronization puts on-premises users and groups into Microsoft Entra ID, and two engines can do it. Microsoft Entra Connect Sync is a full sync server installed on-premises; it reaches every connected forest from that server and supports the widest range of advanced scenarios. Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync moves the orchestration into the cloud and needs only lightweight provisioning agents that make outbound connections, update themselves and fail over automatically when several are installed. Its standout capability is synchronizing disconnected forests, such as those of acquired companies that have no trust or network path to each other. A design question usually gives away the answer: many isolated forests, a light footprint and high availability through extra agents point to Cloud Sync, while a single sync server with deep customization points to Connect Sync. Both work with PHS and PTA, and the two can run side by side during a migration.

concepts.heading: MFA and Conditional Access
concepts.body: Conditional Access is the policy engine of Microsoft Entra ID: if a sign-in matches conditions such as user or group, app, location, device platform or risk, then grant controls apply, such as requiring MFA, a compliant device or an authentication strength, or the sign-in is blocked. It needs Microsoft Entra ID P1. Risk-based policies use Microsoft Entra ID Protection signals: sign-in risk estimates whether this sign-in is not the owner, user risk whether the account is compromised, and they need P2. Authentication strengths say which methods satisfy a policy. The built-in Phishing-resistant MFA strength accepts only Windows Hello for Business or platform credentials, FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, and multifactor certificate-based authentication, so it can be required for administrators while other staff keep the normal MFA strength. Learn also asks for two or more cloud-only emergency access accounts with separate phishing-resistant credentials, excluded from policies that block sign-in.

concepts.heading: Passwordless Methods and Onboarding
concepts.body: Passwordless sign-in removes the password from the sign-in itself. Windows Hello for Business binds a credential to a user's device and unlocks it with a PIN or biometrics. FIDO2 security keys and passkeys use public key cryptography tied to the real site, which makes them phishing-resistant. Certificate-based authentication suits organizations that already issue smart cards. Microsoft Authenticator phone sign-in also avoids the password and meets the Passwordless MFA strength, but it is not counted as phishing-resistant. Getting users onto these methods is a design question in its own right. A Temporary Access Pass is a time-limited passcode, single use or multi-use, that an administrator issues so a new user can sign in for the first time and register a passkey or Windows Hello without ever having a password; it also helps recovery when a user loses a strong method. SMS and voice remain usable as MFA methods but are the weakest choices.

concepts.heading: External Identities
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra External ID covers people outside the workforce, and the design picks the model by who they are. B2B collaboration adds partners as guest users in your workforce tenant; they sign in with their own organization's or identity provider's credentials, and your Conditional Access policies apply to them, with cross-tenant access settings able to trust their home MFA. B2B direct connect creates a mutual trust with another Microsoft Entra organization for Teams shared channels, and those users are not added as guests at all. Cross-tenant synchronization automates creating, updating and removing B2B users between tenants of one multitenant organization, with no invitation emails. For consumers or business customers of your own apps, an external tenant gives self-service sign-up, social identity providers and custom branding, separate from employees. Azure AD B2C is no longer sold to new customers, so new customer-facing designs use External ID in an external tenant.

examPoints: A question about on-premises lockout or logon hours at cloud sign-in points to Pass-through Authentication; least infrastructure, outage survival or leaked credentials point to password hash synchronization.
A question with several disconnected forests and lightweight, self-updating agents is testing Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync rather than Connect Sync.

A question about partners, consumers or sister tenants is testing the External ID model: B2B collaboration for guests, B2B direct connect for Teams shared channels, cross-tenant sync for one organization's tenants, an external tenant for customers.

quiz.q: Engineers of a partner company must work with your staff in Microsoft Teams shared channels. Your security team does not want the partner's users created as guest accounts in your directory, and both organizations use Microsoft Entra ID. What should you recommend?
choices: Set up B2B direct connect with the partner organization through cross-tenant access settings for Teams shared channels
Invite each partner engineer as a B2B collaboration guest and add the guests to the teams that hold the shared channels
Create an external tenant with self-service sign-up so that the partner engineers can register their own accounts for Teams
Configure cross-tenant synchronization so that partner accounts are created and removed automatically in your workforce tenant
quiz.explain: B2B direct connect is a mutual trust between two Microsoft Entra organizations that lets users join Teams shared channels without being added as guests. Choice D is tempting because it automates the accounts, but cross-tenant synchronization still creates B2B users in your directory and is meant for tenants of the same organization.

quiz.q: New hires must register a passkey on their first day without ever being given a password, and the help desk should be able to restore access the same way when a user loses a security key. What should you recommend?
choices: Send each new hire an initial password by text message and require them to replace it with a passkey at the first sign-in
Enable SMS sign-in for new hires so that they can sign in with a one-time code and then register a passkey on their own later
Issue a Temporary Access Pass to each new hire and lost-key user so they can sign in once and register their passkey right away
Create the accounts as cloud-only emergency access accounts so that new hires can sign in without MFA until a passkey is set up
quiz.explain: A Temporary Access Pass is a time-limited passcode made for onboarding and recovering strong methods, so users register a passkey without a password. Choice B is tempting because SMS sign-in also avoids a password, but it is a weak method and does not give the help desk a controlled, time-limited recovery path.

days.recap: Pick PHS for simplicity and resilience or PTA for on-premises policy at sign-in, Cloud Sync for disconnected forests, Conditional Access with authentication strengths and risk for MFA decisions, a Temporary Access Pass to onboard passwordless methods, and the External ID model that matches who the external users are.

days.title: Authorization Design: Azure RBAC, Custom Roles, Managed Identities, PIM and Access to On-premises Apps

concepts.heading: Two Role Systems: Azure RBAC and Microsoft Entra Roles
concepts.body: Azure has two separate role systems, and many design questions hinge on picking the right one. Azure RBAC controls Azure resources: a role assignment joins a security principal, a role definition such as Reader, Contributor, Owner or User Access Administrator, and a scope (management group, subscription, resource group or resource), and it is inherited by every child scope. Permissions are additive; explicit deny assignments exist but are created by Azure features such as deployment stacks, not by hand. Microsoft Entra roles, such as Global Administrator, User Administrator or Helpdesk Administrator, control the directory itself: users, groups, app registrations and passwords. A help desk that resets passwords needs an Entra role and no Azure role, while a team that restarts VMs needs an Azure role and no Entra role. Least privilege means the narrowest role at the lowest scope that still covers all targets, and groups rather than individual users as assignees.

concepts.heading: Custom Roles and Conditions
concepts.body: When no built-in role is narrow enough, a custom role lists exactly the operations needed. Its JSON has Actions and NotActions for the control plane, DataActions and NotDataActions for data such as blob contents, and AssignableScopes that say where it may be assigned, which can include a management group. For example, an operator role with read access plus start, restart and deallocate on VMs, assigned once at a management group, covers every current and future subscription below it. NotActions is not a deny: it only subtracts from that role, so another assignment can still grant the operation. Azure attribute-based access control adds conditions to a role assignment, for example allowing blob reads only when the blob's Project index tag matches a value; this gives fine-grained access with far fewer role assignments, which matters because subscriptions have an assignment limit. Conditions filter what a role grants; they cannot express an explicit deny.

concepts.heading: Managed Identities and Workload Identity Federation
concepts.body: Applications should not hold secrets to reach Azure resources. A managed identity gives an Azure resource an identity in Microsoft Entra ID whose credentials Azure manages and rotates. A system-assigned identity is created and deleted with its resource and used only by it, which is ideal when audit logs must show which resource acted and when permissions should vanish with the resource. A user-assigned identity is a standalone resource that many resources can share, which suits identical scale-out instances, role assignments that must exist before deployment, and organizations that require approval for each new identity. Workloads outside Azure, such as GitHub Actions, or pods in AKS, use workload identity federation: the external platform's token is exchanged for a Microsoft Entra token through a federated credential on a user-assigned identity or app registration, so no secret is stored or rotated. On AKS this is Microsoft Entra Workload ID, which maps a Kubernetes service account to that identity.

concepts.heading: Privileged Identity Management
concepts.body: Standing privileged access is a risk: a compromised permanent Owner has full control at any hour. Privileged Identity Management (PIM) replaces permanent assignments with eligible ones that a user activates only when needed. Activation can require a justification, MFA, approval by designated approvers and a maximum duration after which the role is removed automatically, and every activation is audited. PIM covers Microsoft Entra roles, Azure resource roles such as Owner on a subscription, and PIM for Groups, where membership of a group that holds several roles becomes just-in-time. Assignments can also have start and end dates, which suits contractors, and access reviews can recertify who should stay eligible. PIM needs Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Microsoft Entra ID Governance licenses. In the exam, wording such as just-in-time, approval, time-limited or no standing access almost always points to PIM rather than to custom roles or Conditional Access.

concepts.heading: Reaching On-premises and Legacy Apps
concepts.body: Two services bring older applications into a Microsoft Entra design. Microsoft Entra application proxy publishes on-premises web apps to remote users without a VPN or inbound firewall ports: a lightweight private network connector inside the network makes only outbound connections to the cloud service. Users authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID first, so Conditional Access and MFA apply before any traffic reaches the app, and for apps using Integrated Windows Authentication the connector signs users in with Kerberos constrained delegation. Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides a managed domain in an Azure virtual network with domain join, Group Policy, LDAP and Kerberos or NTLM, without deploying or patching domain controllers. It syncs one way from Microsoft Entra ID, so users keep their credentials; synced hybrid users need password hash synchronization for this. Choose application proxy for publishing web apps, Domain Services for workloads in Azure that need classic domain protocols.

examPoints: A question about managing users, passwords or app registrations is testing Microsoft Entra roles; one about managing Azure resources at a scope is testing Azure RBAC.

A question with shared access for many identical resources points to a user-assigned managed identity, per-resource auditing or cleanup to system-assigned, and a workload outside Azure or a pod in AKS to workload identity federation.

A question with just-in-time, approval or time-limited elevation is testing PIM; remote access to an on-premises web app without inbound ports is application proxy, and LDAP or Kerberos in Azure without domain controllers is Domain Services.

quiz.q: A service desk team must reset forgotten passwords for ordinary employees. It must not change any Azure resources or manage administrator accounts. What should you recommend?
choices: Assign the Contributor Azure role at the root management group so that the team can manage the user accounts in every subscription
Create a custom Azure role with the user write actions and assign it at the tenant root so that it applies to every directory user
Assign the User Access Administrator Azure role on each subscription so that the team can manage access and accounts for employees
Assign the Helpdesk Administrator Microsoft Entra role to the team, which resets passwords for non-administrators in the directory
quiz.explain: Password resets are directory operations, so they belong to a Microsoft Entra role, and Helpdesk Administrator covers non-administrator users without touching Azure resources. Choice C is tempting because its name mentions access, but User Access Administrator manages Azure role assignments, not user accounts or passwords.

quiz.q: Microservices in an AKS cluster must read secrets from Azure Key Vault. Security forbids storing client secrets or certificates in the cluster, and each microservice must have its own permissions. What should you recommend?
choices: Create one service principal with a client secret for the whole cluster and store that secret as a Kubernetes secret in each namespace
Use Microsoft Entra Workload ID, federating each microservice's service account with its own user-assigned managed identity
Assign the Key Vault Secrets User role to the cluster's node pool identity so that every pod on the nodes can read the vault secrets
Enable access policies on the vault and grant Get permission to the virtual network that the AKS cluster nodes are connected to
quiz.explain: Workload ID exchanges a Kubernetes service account token for a Microsoft Entra token, so no secret is stored and each microservice gets its own identity and role assignments. Choice C is tempting because it also avoids secrets, but the node identity is shared by every pod, which breaks the per-microservice permission requirement.

days.recap: Use Microsoft Entra roles for the directory and Azure RBAC for resources, custom roles and conditions for narrow access, managed identities or workload identity federation instead of secrets, PIM for just-in-time privilege, and application proxy or Domain Services to reach older apps.

days.title: Secrets, Keys and Certificates: Key Vault Tiers, Managed HSM and the Access Model

concepts.heading: What Key Vault Stores and Which Container to Pick
concepts.body: Azure Key Vault keeps three kinds of objects. Secrets are values such as connection strings and API keys; keys are cryptographic keys used for encryption, signing and wrapping, often as customer-managed keys for other Azure services; certificates are X.509 certificates whose lifecycle Key Vault can manage. There are two container types. Vaults come in Standard, with software-protected keys, and Premium, which adds HSM-protected keys, and both are multitenant services. Managed HSM pools are a fully managed, single-tenant service that holds only HSM-backed keys, with a customer-specific security domain and its own local RBAC, so designated HSM administrators keep control that subscription Owners cannot override. Learn notes that the HSM fleet for both Premium and Managed HSM now runs FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated firmware, so the deciding requirement for Managed HSM is dedicated tenancy and the customer-owned security domain, not FIPS alone.

concepts.heading: RBAC or Access Policies
concepts.body: A vault's data plane can be authorized in two ways. The legacy access policy model grants permissions per principal in the vault itself, but anyone with write access to the vault resource, such as Contributor, can add a policy and give themselves access to secrets, and it does not work with PIM. The Azure RBAC model, which Learn recommends and which is the default for new vaults in recent API versions, uses role assignments: Key Vault Administrator for full data plane management, Key Vault Secrets Officer and Secrets User for managing or reading secrets, Key Vault Crypto Officer for keys, Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User for services that wrap and unwrap with a customer-managed key, and Key Vault Certificates Officer for certificates. Granting data access then needs Owner or User Access Administrator, roles can be scoped down to a single secret, and PIM can make administrator access just-in-time. Applications should reach the vault with a managed identity, not a stored secret.

concepts.heading: Protecting Against Deletion and Rotating Safely
concepts.body: Soft delete keeps deleted vaults and objects recoverable for 7 to 90 days; it is on by default and cannot be turned off. Purge protection, which is optional, stops anyone, administrators included, from permanently purging a deleted vault or object before that retention period ends. Learn recommends it whenever keys encrypt data, and services such as Azure Storage require it for customer-managed keys, because a purged key would make the data unreadable forever. For keys, a rotation policy creates a new version on a schedule and can raise an Event Grid notification before expiry. Services configured with the versionless key URI pick up the newest version automatically, while existing data stays tied to the version that encrypted it. For secrets used by App Service, Functions or Logic Apps, a Key Vault reference without a version follows rotation too: the platform caches values and picks up the latest version within 24 hours, or immediately after a configuration change.

concepts.heading: Certificates
concepts.body: Key Vault can create, import, store and renew certificates. A certificate policy sets the subject, key type and size, validity period and lifetime actions. A lifetime action is triggered a number of days before expiry or at a percentage of the lifetime, and it either emails contacts or auto-renews. Automatic renewal works when the issuer is one of Key Vault's partner certificate authorities, DigiCert or GlobalSign, configured as an issuer object with the account credentials; certificates from other, non-partnered authorities can be stored but must be renewed outside Key Vault. Self-signed certificates can also be issued and renewed for internal use. Services such as App Service and Application Gateway can import a certificate from Key Vault through a managed identity and follow renewals, so nobody has to upload a new PFX file. In a design question, a requirement for TLS certificates that renew without manual steps points to a Key Vault certificate with a partner issuer and an auto-renew lifetime action.

concepts.heading: Vault Layout and Network Isolation
concepts.body: Learn's guidance is one vault per application, per environment and per region. Separate vaults limit the blast radius of a breach and keep teams' administrative rights apart, because with the RBAC model administrative tasks such as network rules and monitoring need vault-level permissions. On the network side, a private endpoint gives the vault a private IP address in a virtual network, and the vault firewall can then disable public access or allow only selected networks; the trusted Microsoft services exception lets certain platform services through the firewall. Diagnostic settings should send the AuditEvent logs to a Log Analytics workspace so every access to keys and secrets can be queried and alerted on, and Azure Policy can enforce purge protection, the RBAC model and private access across all vaults. Microsoft Defender for Key Vault adds detection of unusual access patterns on top of these controls.

examPoints: A question that requires single-tenant HSMs, a customer-controlled security domain or key admins that subscription Owners cannot override is testing Managed HSM; HSM-protected keys in a multitenant vault are Key Vault Premium.
A question about stopping contributors from granting themselves secret access, or about just-in-time vault administration, is testing the Azure RBAC permission model with PIM.

A question about surviving malicious deletion of an encryption key is testing purge protection, and one about rotation without outages is testing versionless key URIs, versionless Key Vault references and auto-renewing certificates.

quiz.q: A public website on App Service uses a TLS certificate that the team renews by hand every year, and it has expired twice. The company buys its certificates from DigiCert. What should you recommend so renewal happens without manual steps?
choices: Store the certificate as a secret in Key Vault and create an alert rule that emails the team a month before the certificate expires
Create the certificate in Key Vault with DigiCert as the issuer and an auto-renew lifetime action, and bind it to App Service
Export the certificate to a storage account each year and let an Azure Automation runbook upload it to App Service on a schedule
Replace the certificate with a self-signed certificate created in Key Vault, because only self-signed certificates can auto-renew
quiz.explain: DigiCert is a Key Vault partner issuer, so a certificate policy with an auto-renew lifetime action renews it, and App Service follows the new version through its Key Vault binding. Choice D is tempting because Key Vault can renew self-signed certificates, but browsers do not trust them on a public website, and partner CA certificates renew too.

quiz.q: A web app on App Service reads a database password from a Key Vault reference that includes a specific secret version. After the security team rotated the password, the app kept using the old value. What should you recommend so future rotations need no app change?
choices: Remove the version from the Key Vault reference so that the app resolves the latest secret version, using its managed identity
Copy the new password into a plain app setting after each rotation, because Key Vault references cannot follow secret versions
Move the password into a Managed HSM pool, because App Service follows rotated secrets automatically only in Managed HSM
Switch the vault to the access policy model, because only access policies allow App Service to read newer versions of secrets
quiz.explain: A versioned reference pins one value; without a version the platform resolves the latest version and refreshes it within 24 hours or on the next configuration change. Choice C is tempting because Managed HSM sounds stronger, but it stores only keys, not secrets, so it cannot hold the password at all.

days.recap: Pick Standard, Premium or Managed HSM by protection and tenancy needs, authorize with Azure RBAC and managed identities, turn on purge protection for encryption keys, rotate through versionless URIs and references, auto-renew certificates with partner issuers, and keep one private, monitored vault per app, environment and region.

days.title: Governance Design: Hierarchy, Tags, Azure Policy, Compliance, Identity Governance, Locks and Deployment Stacks

concepts.heading: Management Groups, Subscriptions and Resource Groups
concepts.body: Each level of the hierarchy has its own job. Management groups gather subscriptions that need the same governance; policy and role assignments made there are inherited by every child, including subscriptions added later, and subscription owners cannot remove them. The tree can be six levels deep below the tenant root. New subscriptions land under the root by default, so Microsoft recommends a default management group such as sandbox and requiring authorization to create management groups. Subscriptions are the boundary for quotas, billing and a clean access split: the Cloud Adoption Framework says not to build management groups for development, test and production, but to use separate subscriptions in the same management group so all environments inherit the same policies. Resource groups hold resources that share a lifecycle: deployed, updated and deleted together.

concepts.heading: Tags and Azure Policy
concepts.body: Tags are name-value pairs that drive cost reporting and operations, but resources do not inherit tags from their resource group or subscription, and tag values are case-sensitive, so Finance and finance become separate rows in a cost report. Azure Policy fixes both: a deny rule can require a tag or an allowed list of values, and a modify rule can copy a tag from the resource group. Policy evaluates what resources look like, whoever creates them, while Azure RBAC decides who may act; allowed regions, SKUs and VM sizes are therefore policy. Effects include deny, audit, append, modify, auditIfNotExists, deployIfNotExists and denyAction, which blocks deletes of matching resources while still allowing updates. Modify and deployIfNotExists use the assignment's managed identity, and resources that already exist are fixed with a remediation task. Initiatives group definitions, and a custom definition must be saved at a management group that contains every subscription where it will be assigned.

concepts.heading: Rolling Out Policy and Proving Compliance
concepts.body: A new assignment can run with enforcement mode DoNotEnforce, which evaluates compliance without blocking anything, and then be switched to Default once results are clean. Exemptions record a justified exception on one resource or scope, with a category of waiver or mitigated and an optional expiry date, while staying visible in compliance reports. For settings inside operating systems, Azure Machine Configuration audits or applies guest settings, such as TLS versions, on Azure VMs and Azure Arc-enabled servers. Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides the regulatory compliance dashboard: the Microsoft cloud security benchmark is on by default, and adding standards such as PCI DSS or ISO 27001 needs at least one paid plan. That data surfaces in Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager, which manages compliance across Microsoft 365 and cloud resources. Microsoft Purview Data Map governs the data itself, scanning and classifying sensitive data across hybrid and multicloud sources with lineage. Azure Resource Graph queries resource properties across all subscriptions in seconds.

concepts.heading: Identity Governance
concepts.body: Microsoft Entra ID Governance controls who keeps access over time. Access reviews ask reviewers, such as group owners, managers or the users themselves, to recertify group memberships, app assignments and roles on a schedule, and they can apply results automatically. Reviews scoped to guests can block denied guests from signing in for 30 days and then remove them from the tenant. Multi-stage reviews run reviewers in sequence, so an application owner sees only what managers approved; in a single-stage review the last decision wins. Entitlement management bundles groups, Teams, SharePoint sites and apps into access packages, with policies for who may request, who approves and when access expires; users from connected organizations who are not yet in the directory are invited automatically on approval and removed when access ends. Lifecycle workflows automate joiner, mover and leaver tasks from HR attributes such as the hire and leave dates, for example sending a Temporary Access Pass to a manager before day one.

concepts.heading: Locks, Deployment Stacks and the End of Blueprints
concepts.body: Resource locks protect the control plane for everyone, Owners included, and are inherited by child scopes. CanNotDelete still allows updates, while ReadOnly blocks every change and has side effects: a ReadOnly lock on a resource group with an App Service plan prevents scaling it. Deployment stacks manage the resources from one Bicep file or ARM template as a unit at resource group, subscription or management group scope. Deny settings, DenyDelete or DenyWriteAndDelete, place a deny assignment on the managed resources that even subscription Owners cannot bypass, with up to five excluded principals such as the pipeline identity; Learn recommends placing the stack at the parent scope so subscription Owners cannot edit it. actionOnUnmanage decides whether resources dropped from the template are detached or deleted. Azure Blueprints is a preview being retired, with final retirement on January 31, 2027; designs use deployment stacks and template specs instead.

examPoints: A question about applying rules to many current and future subscriptions is testing management group inheritance; separate environments with their own quotas and costs are separate subscriptions in the same management group.

A question about what resources may look like (regions, SKUs, required tags) is testing Azure Policy, with modify or deployIfNotExists plus remediation for existing resources; a question about who may act is testing RBAC.
A question that mentions Blueprints-style locking, protecting platform resources from subscription Owners, or deleting a deployment as one unit is testing deployment stacks.

quiz.q: A platform team used Azure Blueprints to deploy a hub network into each new subscription and lock it against changes by application teams. The team must move to a supported approach before Blueprints is retired. What should you recommend?
choices: Keep the blueprint assignments and add ReadOnly locks to the hub network resource groups so that the locking survives the retirement
Replace the blueprints with Azure Policy deployIfNotExists definitions, which create the hub network and prevent any later changes
Deploy the hub network from Bicep as a deployment stack with deny settings, shared as a template spec across subscriptions
Create a custom RBAC role without network write actions and assign it at the root, so that nobody can change any hub network again
quiz.explain: Learn names deployment stacks and template specs as the successor: the stack deploys the resources and its deny settings protect them from subscription Owners, with the pipeline identity excluded. Choice B is tempting because deployIfNotExists can deploy resources, but it does not stop teams from changing or deleting them afterwards.

quiz.q: A security officer must find, within minutes, every virtual machine across 180 subscriptions that has no Owner tag, sorted by subscription, so the teams can be contacted. No change to the resources is needed. What should you recommend?
choices: Create a new Azure Policy assignment with the deny effect for the Owner tag and wait for the next compliance scan to list the VMs
Export the activity log of every subscription to one workspace and search for VM creation events that did not include an Owner tag
Run a remediation task with a modify policy that adds an Owner tag of Unknown to every VM, and then list the VMs with that value
Run an Azure Resource Graph query across the subscriptions that filters virtual machines on a missing Owner tag and groups the results
quiz.explain: Resource Graph queries the current properties of resources across many subscriptions at once, so a single query lists untagged VMs by subscription without changing anything. Choice A is tempting because policy reports compliance, but a deny effect only blocks new requests and the evaluation is slower than a direct query.

days.recap: Use management groups for inherited governance, subscriptions as environment and billing boundaries and resource groups by lifecycle; enforce tags and resource shapes with Azure Policy, prove compliance with Defender for Cloud and Purview, govern access with reviews, access packages and lifecycle workflows, and protect deployments with locks and deployment stacks instead of Blueprints.

days.title: Relational Options and Tiers: SQL Database, Managed Instance, SQL Server on VMs, vCore and DTU, Hyperscale, Serverless and Elastic Pools
services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

concepts.heading: Three Ways to Run SQL Server in Azure
concepts.body: The first design decision is how much of SQL Server you need to control. Azure SQL Database is PaaS at the database level: Microsoft runs the engine, patching, backups and high availability, and you get features such as serverless and Hyperscale, but instance-scoped features are missing, including SQL Server Agent (elastic jobs replace it), cross-database queries with three-part names, CLR and Database Mail. Azure SQL Managed Instance is PaaS at the instance level with near-complete compatibility with SQL Server: Agent, cross-database queries, CLR, Service Broker, linked servers, distributed transactions and native restore of .bak files from Blob storage all work, and it is deployed into your own virtual network subnet. SQL Server on Azure VMs is IaaS with full engine and operating system control, needed for FILESTREAM, software on the same server such as SSRS or SSAS, older SQL Server versions or OS-level agents. The trade-off is simple: more control means more operations work for your team.

concepts.heading: vCore or DTU
concepts.body: Azure SQL Database offers two purchasing models. The DTU model sells preconfigured bundles of compute, memory and I/O in the Basic, Standard and Premium tiers, with storage included and no choice of hardware; it is simple for small, steady databases. The vCore model, which Microsoft recommends, lets you choose vCores, hardware and storage independently in the General Purpose, Business Critical or Hyperscale tier. Only the vCore model offers Azure Hybrid Benefit, which reuses SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance (not for new Hyperscale databases, which have no SQL license fee), and reserved capacity, and it also unlocks serverless compute and Hyperscale. SQL Managed Instance uses the vCore model only. A requirement that mentions existing licenses, reservations, independent scaling of compute and storage, or a need to compare sizes with on-premises cores is a signal for vCore. A requirement for the simplest fixed bundle for a small database is the only common case where DTU still fits, and you can move a database between the models later.

concepts.heading: General Purpose, Business Critical and Hyperscale
concepts.body: The vCore tiers differ in storage design. General Purpose keeps data files on remote premium storage, has no readable replica and suits most business workloads at the lowest vCore cost. Business Critical runs a cluster of replicas on locally attached SSD with storage latency of about 1-2 ms, supports In-Memory OLTP tables and includes one readable secondary for read scale-out at no extra charge. Both cap a database at 4 TB. Hyperscale separates compute from a distributed storage layer that grows automatically up to 128 TB; backups and restores are file snapshots that take minutes whatever the size and put no load on compute, and it adds up to four high-availability replicas and up to 30 named replicas for reads. Microsoft calls Hyperscale the recommended default for new OLTP workloads. Leaving it is limited: reverse migration only goes to General Purpose and only within 45 days of the original conversion, so test early.

concepts.heading: Serverless Compute
concepts.body: Within the vCore model, Azure SQL Database single databases can use provisioned or serverless compute. Provisioned compute is a fixed size billed every hour, busy or idle, and fits regular, predictable load. Serverless sets a minimum and maximum vCore range; compute scales automatically inside it and is billed per second for what is used, and after an auto-pause delay with no activity the database pauses so only storage is billed, resuming on the next connection. Microsoft recommends serverless for a single database with intermittent, unpredictable use and for new databases without usage history. The trade-offs are a warm-up delay after pauses and memory trimming, and Learn says provisioned compute gives better price-performance for regular use with high average utilization. Auto-pause can also be disabled when a resume delay is unacceptable; scaling still follows load. Serverless is available in General Purpose and Hyperscale (where auto-pause is still in preview), but not in Business Critical, and it does not apply to SQL Managed Instance.

concepts.heading: Elastic Pools
concepts.body: An elastic pool buys one amount of resources, in eDTUs or vCores, and shares it among many databases on the same logical server. Each database bursts when it needs to and uses almost nothing when idle, and the pool is billed per hour regardless of how many databases it holds. Microsoft's ideal candidates have a large gap between peak and average use, peaks at different times from each other, and enough databases to share the capacity, which describes many SaaS designs with a database per tenant. Databases with persistent medium-high use gain nothing from sharing and should stay single. Per-database minimum and maximum settings stop one noisy database from starving others. Serverless and pools solve similar problems differently: serverless optimizes one intermittent database, while Microsoft's serverless guidance says many intermittent databases usually get better price-performance from a provisioned elastic pool. SQL Managed Instance offers instance pools for small instances, a separate feature.

examPoints: A question listing SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries, CLR, Service Broker or native .bak restore with no operating system to manage is testing SQL Managed Instance; FILESTREAM or OS access needs SQL Server on Azure VMs.

A question about license reuse, reservations or sizing compute and storage separately is testing the vCore model; growth beyond 4 TB or fast snapshot restores is Hyperscale; low latency, In-Memory OLTP and a free readable replica is Business Critical.
A question about one intermittent database is testing serverless, and one about many databases with low average use and non-overlapping peaks is testing elastic pools.

quiz.q: A company is moving a reporting application to Azure. It runs SQL Server Reporting Services on the same server as its database engine and relies on a monitoring agent installed in the operating system. It wants as few changes as possible. Which option should you recommend?
choices: Azure SQL Database in the Business Critical tier with read scale-out, so the reports run on the readable secondary replica
Azure SQL Managed Instance in the General Purpose tier, so that instance-level features like SQL Server Agent stay available
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale with a named replica that hosts the Reporting Services workload apart from the primary replica
SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine, which keeps Reporting Services on the same server and gives full operating system access
quiz.explain: Running SSRS on the same server and installing agents in the operating system both need a server you control, which only SQL Server on an Azure VM provides. Choice B is tempting because Managed Instance supports nearly all engine features, but it gives no operating system access and cannot host Reporting Services on the instance.

quiz.q: A company has 25 Azure SQL databases, each running at steady medium-to-high CPU throughout the business day. An architect proposes putting them into one elastic pool to save money. What should you advise?
choices: Keep them as single databases sized for their load, because databases with persistent medium-high use gain little from sharing
Put them in one elastic pool, because any group of more than 20 databases always costs less in a pool than as single databases
Move all of them to serverless compute, because serverless is cheaper than provisioned compute for databases that are busy all day
Convert them to Hyperscale and add named replicas, because Hyperscale removes the compute cost of databases that run all day long
quiz.explain: Pools save money when peaks are short, far above the average and at different times; databases that are busy together would need a pool as large as their combined load. Choice C is tempting because serverless also targets cost, but Learn optimizes it for intermittent use with low average utilization; steady busy databases get better price-performance from provisioned compute.

days.recap: Choose SQL Database, Managed Instance or SQL Server on VMs by how much instance and OS control the workload needs; prefer the vCore model; pick General Purpose, Business Critical or Hyperscale by latency, size and replicas; and use serverless for one intermittent database and elastic pools for many.

days.title: Relational Scalability and Protection: Read Scale-out, Sharding, Encryption, Masking, Ledger and PostgreSQL or MySQL Flexible Server

concepts.heading: Scaling Reads
concepts.body: Before adding databases, use the replicas you already have. In Business Critical and Premium, read scale-out sends connections with ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly to a secondary replica at no extra charge. Hyperscale high-availability replicas accept the same read-only connections, and named replicas, up to 30, each have their own name, compute size and endpoint, so separate teams can run heavy reads without competing with each other or with the primary. Active geo-replication in Azure SQL Database adds readable secondary databases in other regions, up to four, which serve distant readers and are also a disaster recovery target; failover groups add a listener endpoint that follows a failover. All of these secondaries are asynchronous, so data can lag the primary slightly, which suits reports and dashboards but not logic that must read its own writes immediately. General Purpose has no free readable replica, so reads there need a geo-secondary or a different tier.

concepts.heading: Scaling Out with Sharding
concepts.body: When one database cannot hold the data or the transaction throughput, or tenants need isolation or specific geographies, the design spreads data across many databases with the same schema. The Elastic Database client library keeps a shard map that routes each request by a sharding key such as the tenant ID, and transactions should stay within one key value. Common SaaS layouts mix single-tenant databases for large customers with multitenant databases for small ones, and the split-merge tool moves a tenant between shards, for example from a shared trial database to its own database. Elastic jobs roll schema changes out to every shard, and elastic pools keep the many databases affordable. Sharding adds application complexity, so it is the answer only when scaling up, read replicas or Hyperscale are not enough. For PostgreSQL, elastic clusters in Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server provide managed Citus sharding across nodes, with row-based or schema-based distribution and online rebalancing when nodes are added.

concepts.heading: Encryption: TDE and Always Encrypted
concepts.body: Transparent data encryption (TDE) encrypts database files, logs and backups at rest with no application change. By default the protector is managed by Microsoft; with customer-managed TDE the protector is a key in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM that the customer rotates, audits and can revoke, which makes the databases inaccessible. TDE protects against stolen files, but data is decrypted in memory for anyone with database permissions. Always Encrypted protects specific columns even from DBAs and cloud operators: the client driver encrypts and decrypts values, and the column master key stays outside the database, for example in Key Vault. Deterministic encryption allows equality lookups, joins and grouping but can reveal patterns; randomized encryption is safer but allows no operations without a secure enclave. Always Encrypted with secure enclaves lets the engine run range comparisons, sorting and pattern matching inside a protected memory region. Choose TDE for at-rest compliance, Always Encrypted when even privileged insiders must not see values.

concepts.heading: Masking, Row-level Security, Auditing and Ledger
concepts.body: Several controls limit what users see or prove what happened. Dynamic data masking hides values in query results for non-privileged users, for example showing only the last four digits of a card, with no application changes; it is not encryption, administrators and users with UNMASK still see real data, and ad hoc queries can infer values, so it limits casual exposure only. Row-level security uses filter and block predicates so the database itself returns and accepts only the rows a session may access, such as one tenant's rows, however a query is written. Auditing records database events to a Log Analytics workspace for KQL and alerts, to Event Hubs for a SIEM, and to storage, where an immutability policy with protected append writes gives a tamper-proof copy. Ledger tables hash every change and chain transactions, with digests stored outside the database in immutable storage, so any tampering, even by DBAs, can be detected and proven to auditors.

concepts.heading: PostgreSQL and MySQL Flexible Server
concepts.body: Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure Database for MySQL use the flexible server model, with three compute tiers: Burstable for development and low-use servers on a CPU credit model, General Purpose for most production work, and Memory Optimized for memory-heavy workloads. A server can be stopped and started on demand, and compute billing stops while it is stopped. High availability keeps a synchronous standby, in another availability zone for zone-redundant HA or in the same zone, with automatic failover; the standby cannot serve reads. Read replicas are separate, asynchronous, read-only servers for reporting or distant readers, supported on General Purpose and Memory Optimized but not Burstable; MySQL allows up to 10 and suggests a proxy such as ProxySQL to split reads and writes. A replica can be promoted for disaster recovery. Choose flexible server when an application already uses open-source PostgreSQL or MySQL, and elastic clusters when PostgreSQL outgrows one server.

examPoints: A question about offloading reads without a new database is testing read scale-out in Business Critical or Hyperscale; separate, sized read workloads point to Hyperscale named replicas and distant readers to geo-replication.

A question about owning and revoking the at-rest key is testing customer-managed TDE; hiding values from DBAs is Always Encrypted; partial display without app changes is dynamic data masking; tenant isolation in a shared schema is row-level security; proving no tampering is ledger.
A question about PostgreSQL or MySQL is testing flexible server tiers, zone-redundant HA whose standby is not readable, and read replicas that need General Purpose or Memory Optimized.

quiz.q: An order system runs on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server in the General Purpose tier. The business requires that the database keeps running with automatic failover if one availability zone in the region fails. What should you recommend?
choices: Enable zone-redundant high availability, which keeps a synchronous standby in another zone and fails over automatically
Add a read replica in another availability zone and point the application to it manually whenever the primary zone fails
Change the server to the Burstable tier and enable stop and start, so that it can be restarted in a different availability zone
Shard the database with elastic clusters so that each node runs in a different zone and the data survives a single zone failure
quiz.explain: Zone-redundant HA places a synchronously replicated standby in a second zone and fails over to it automatically. Choice B is tempting because a replica can be promoted, but replication is asynchronous and promotion is a manual step, so it gives neither automatic failover nor a guarantee of no data loss.

quiz.q: A global retailer runs its order database on Azure SQL Database in West Europe. Analysts in Southeast Asia need fast read-only access for dashboards, and the company also wants a copy in another region that it can fail over to after a regional outage. What should you recommend?
choices: Enable read scale-out in Business Critical so that analysts in Southeast Asia connect to the database's built-in secondary
Add Hyperscale named replicas in West Europe and route the Southeast Asia analysts to them through the database's private endpoint
Create an active geo-replication secondary in Southeast Asia, readable by the analysts and available as a failover target
Copy the database to Southeast Asia every night with an export and import job, and let analysts query the most recent copy
quiz.explain: A geo-secondary is a readable database in another region, so it serves distant analysts and also gives a disaster recovery target. Choice A is tempting because read scale-out is free, but its secondary replica sits in the same region as the primary, so it helps neither Asian latency nor a regional outage.

days.recap: Scale reads with read scale-out, named replicas and geo-secondaries, shard only when one database is not enough, protect data with TDE, Always Encrypted, masking, row-level security, auditing and ledger as each requirement demands, and run open-source engines on flexible server with zone-redundant HA and read replicas.

days.title: Azure Cosmos DB Design: APIs, Partitioning, Consistency Levels and Throughput Modes

concepts.heading: Choosing an API
concepts.body: Azure Cosmos DB runs several APIs on the same globally distributed engine, and the choice follows the application rather than the data. The API for NoSQL is the native one, storing JSON items and querying them with a SQL-like language; Learn points new cloud-native applications to it because it gets the broadest feature set first. The wire-compatible APIs exist so existing applications keep their drivers and query languages: the API for MongoDB for MongoDB apps, the API for Apache Cassandra for wide-column CQL workloads such as telemetry, the API for Apache Gremlin for graph traversals, and the API for Table for apps written against Azure Table storage that need global distribution, more throughput options or automatic indexing on every property. The API is chosen when the account is created and cannot be changed later. In a design scenario, keeping existing drivers with minimal code changes points to the matching wire-compatible API, while a new app with no legacy constraint points to NoSQL.

concepts.heading: Partition Keys
concepts.body: Cosmos DB scales by spreading data across physical partitions. Items with the same partition key value form a logical partition, which can hold at most 20 GB, and each physical partition serves at most 10,000 RU/s, with provisioned throughput divided evenly across physical partitions. A good key has high cardinality, spreads requests evenly so no hot partition takes most of the load, matches the filter of the most frequent queries so they hit one partition instead of fanning out, and never changes, since the key cannot be updated in place. Dates and low-cardinality values such as status or country make poor keys. Hierarchical partition keys allow up to three levels, such as tenant, then user, then session, so one large tenant can grow past 20 GB across several partitions while queries that filter on the tenant still go only to that tenant's partitions. Partition keys, including hierarchical ones, are set when a container is created; changing them means moving data to a new container.

concepts.heading: The Five Consistency Levels
concepts.body: Cosmos DB offers five consistency levels, from strongest to weakest: Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix and Eventual. Strong always returns the latest committed write, but each write must commit in every region, so write latency grows with distance, and it cannot be used with multiple write regions. Strong and Bounded staleness read from two replicas, which doubles the RU cost of reads compared with the weaker levels. Bounded staleness guarantees that reads lag by no more than K versions or T seconds, in order, and fits single-write-region apps that want near-strong reads globally. Session, the default and the most widely used level, guarantees that a client reads its own writes through a session token while other clients may see them a moment later, at weak-level cost. Consistent prefix guarantees order without freshness, and Eventual guarantees neither, for the lowest latency. The account default can be relaxed per request but never made stronger than the default.

concepts.heading: Throughput Modes
concepts.body: Capacity is either provisioned or serverless, chosen per account. Provisioned throughput sets request units per second on a container or on a database shared by its containers, and is billed every hour for what is provisioned. In manual mode you pick a fixed RU/s and change it yourself. Autoscale lets you set a maximum and scales between 10% of that maximum and the maximum, billing each hour for the highest level reached; it suits variable or spiky but sustained traffic and production apps that need predictable performance, and it works with multiple regions. Serverless provisions nothing and bills for the request units actually consumed, which suits development, proofs of concept and apps with intermittent, unpredictable traffic and a low average-to-peak ratio. Its limits matter in a design: a serverless account runs in a single Azure region, so it cannot add regions for global distribution or failover. When traffic is steady and well understood, manual provisioned throughput is the most economical.

concepts.heading: Global Distribution and Data Lifecycle
concepts.body: An account can replicate to any number of regions. With a single write region, other regions serve local reads and can take over as the write region on failover; with multiple write regions, every region accepts writes, which lowers write latency and keeps writes available in a regional outage, at the cost of conflict resolution, last writer wins by default, and no strong consistency. Availability zone support adds resilience inside a region. Data lifecycle features reduce custom code: time to live deletes items automatically a set number of seconds after their last change, configured per container with per-item overrides, and -1 means no expiry unless an item sets its own value. The change feed exposes inserts and updates in order per partition, so Functions or other consumers can update caches, materialized views or downstream systems. For analytics without consuming request units, mirroring into Microsoft Fabric replicates NoSQL containers in near real time; Synapse Link is no longer supported for new projects.

examPoints: A question about moving an existing MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin or Table app with minimal code change is testing the matching Cosmos DB API; a new app with no legacy constraint points to the API for NoSQL.
A question about hot partitions, cross-partition queries or tenants outgrowing 20 GB is testing partition key choice and hierarchical partition keys.

A question about users seeing their own writes cheaply points to Session consistency, a guaranteed maximum lag to Bounded staleness, intermittent single-region traffic to serverless and variable but sustained traffic to autoscale.

quiz.q: A company runs a self-managed MongoDB cluster for a product catalog app. It wants a fully managed, globally distributed Azure database and must keep its existing MongoDB drivers and queries with minimal code changes. Which option should you recommend?
choices: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, rewriting the catalog queries in the SQL-like query language to use the native feature set
Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra, because its wide-column model handles catalog data at high write throughput
Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB, which is wire-compatible so existing drivers and queries keep working with minimal changes
Azure Cosmos DB for Table, because it stores catalog items as key-value entities with automatic indexing on each property
quiz.explain: The API for MongoDB speaks the MongoDB wire protocol, so the existing drivers and queries keep working while Azure manages the service. Choice A is tempting because Learn recommends NoSQL for new apps, but this is a migration, and a rewrite of every query breaks the minimal-change requirement.

quiz.q: A ticketing app on Azure Cosmos DB runs in three regions. Traffic is low at night and climbs to about eight times the baseline every evening, and the app needs predictable performance during the peaks without anyone changing settings by hand. Which capacity option should you recommend?
choices: Serverless capacity mode, so that the account bills only for the request units consumed during the evening peaks
Autoscale provisioned throughput, with the maximum set for the evening peak so RU/s scales down at night by itself
Manual provisioned throughput at the night-time baseline, with requests that exceed it retried by the application code
Manual provisioned throughput sized for the peak, changed by an operator to a lower value each night and back each evening
quiz.explain: Autoscale moves between 10% of the configured maximum and the maximum automatically, so the evening peak is covered and the night costs less, in all three regions. Choice A is tempting because it bills per use, but a serverless account is limited to one region, so it cannot serve this three-region app.

days.recap: Pick the Cosmos DB API by the application's existing protocol, choose a high-cardinality, query-aligned and immutable partition key (hierarchical for large tenants), use Session unless a stronger guarantee is required, and choose serverless, autoscale or manual throughput by traffic shape and region count.

days.title: Unstructured and File Storage: Blob and Data Lake Storage, Access Tiers, Lifecycle, Redundancy, Azure Files and Azure NetApp Files

concepts.heading: Storage Accounts and Data Lake Storage
concepts.body: Most designs start with a standard general-purpose v2 account, which supports blobs, files, queues and tables, every redundancy option and the access tiers. Premium accounts use SSDs for low latency: premium block blob accounts suit high transaction rates or small objects but have no hot, cool, cold or archive tiers, and premium file share accounts host SSD file shares. Azure Data Lake Storage is not a separate service but Blob Storage with the hierarchical namespace enabled. Real directories make renaming or deleting a folder with millions of files one atomic operation, Spark and other Hadoop engines use the ABFS driver, and POSIX-like access control lists on directories and files work together with Azure RBAC for users, groups and managed identities. Blob features such as access tiers and lifecycle management still apply. Choose the hierarchical namespace for analytics data lakes; a flat namespace is fine for application objects, media and backups, where folders are just name prefixes.

concepts.heading: Access Tiers and Rehydration
concepts.body: Blob access tiers trade storage cost against access cost. Hot is for data in active use. Cool, with a 30-day minimum, and cold, with a 90-day minimum, have lower storage and higher access costs, but they are online with the same latency as hot, so rarely read data that must still open instantly belongs there. Archive is offline, with the lowest storage cost and a 180-day minimum: a blob must be rehydrated to an online tier before it can be read. Standard priority rehydration can take up to 15 hours, while high priority can finish in under an hour for objects under 10 GB at a higher cost; copying the blob to a new online blob avoids early deletion charges on the original. Moving or deleting a blob before its minimum period incurs a prorated charge. Archive cannot be the account's default tier, and it is supported only on LRS, GRS and RA-GRS accounts, not on ZRS, GZRS or RA-GZRS accounts.

concepts.heading: Lifecycle Management and Immutability
concepts.body: Lifecycle management policies move or delete blobs automatically. Each rule has filters by prefix or blob index tag, conditions on creation time, last modified time or last access time, and actions such as tier to cool, cold or archive, or delete, for base blobs, versions and snapshots.
