Last access time conditions need access time tracking enabled on the account, and they matter when data is read often but rarely rewritten, because modification time would tier it too early. Rule changes can take up to 24 hours to take effect. For records that nobody may change, immutable storage keeps blobs in a write once, read many state, even against account administrators. Time-based retention policies protect data for a set interval, and once locked they cannot be removed or shortened, which meets regulations such as SEC 17a-4(f); legal holds protect data until they are explicitly cleared. Soft delete and versioning are different: they help recover from mistakes, but administrators can still remove data.

concepts.heading: Redundancy for Durability and Cost
concepts.body: Redundancy choices trade cost against the failures they survive. LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter and is the cheapest, but a datacenter disaster can lose the data. ZRS copies data synchronously across three or more availability zones in the region, so it stays readable and writable when a zone fails and the data never leaves the region, which suits governance rules about location. GRS and GZRS add an asynchronous copy in the paired secondary region, from LRS or ZRS in the primary respectively, so they survive a regional disaster, with possible loss of the most recent writes. The read-access variants, RA-GRS and RA-GZRS, let applications read from the secondary endpoint at any time, without waiting for a failover. Cost rises from LRS to ZRS to GRS to GZRS, and read access adds more. A common design separates accounts: ZRS or GZRS for active data, LRS or GRS for archive data, since archive cannot use zone-redundant options.

concepts.heading: File Services: Azure Files, File Sync and NetApp Files
concepts.body: Azure Files offers fully managed SMB shares on SSD or HDD and NFS 4.1 shares on SSD only, but a share uses one protocol. SMB shares support identity-based access with on-premises AD DS, Microsoft Entra Domain Services or Microsoft Entra Kerberos, and suit lift-and-shift file servers and FSLogix profiles for Azure Virtual Desktop. NFS shares use host-based security, so they always need a private or service endpoint. Azure File Sync turns Windows Servers into caches of an Azure file share: many branch servers can sync to one share, and cloud tiering keeps hot files on local disk while older files become pointers recalled on access. It syncs SMB shares only and has no Linux agent. Azure NetApp Files runs NetApp ONTAP on bare-metal flash in Azure with submillisecond latency, NFSv3, NFSv4.1 and SMB, and dual-protocol volumes that serve Linux and Windows clients at once; it fits HPC, SAP, databases and other demanding enterprise file workloads.

examPoints: A question about directory-level permissions, atomic renames or Spark on files is testing the hierarchical namespace of Data Lake Storage on a general-purpose v2 account.

A question about rarely read data that must open instantly points to cool or cold, data that can wait hours to archive, an urgent archived file to high-priority rehydration, and archive on a zone-redundant account to the LRS, GRS or RA-GRS restriction.

A question about surviving a zone, a region or reading from the secondary is testing ZRS, GRS or GZRS and the RA variants; SMB with AD identities is Azure Files, branch caching is File Sync, and dual-protocol or submillisecond NAS is Azure NetApp Files.

quiz.q: A reporting app stores data in Azure Blob Storage. The data must survive the loss of an availability zone without interruption, and during a regional outage the app must keep reading from another region without waiting for an account failover. Which redundancy option should you recommend?
choices: ZRS, because copying data across three or more zones in the region also gives a readable copy in a second Azure region
RA-GZRS, which replicates across zones in the primary region and allows reads from the secondary region at any time
GRS, because the geo copy in the paired region becomes readable automatically as soon as an outage starts in the primary
LRS in two storage accounts in different regions, with the app writing every blob to both accounts at the same time
quiz.explain: RA-GZRS combines zone-redundant copies in the primary region with a read-access secondary endpoint, so reads continue during a regional outage. Choice C is tempting because GRS has a copy in another region, but without the read-access variant that copy can be read only after a failover.

quiz.q: A company is moving a Windows file server to Azure. Users must keep their mapped drives over SMB, with NTFS-style permissions based on their existing on-premises Active Directory accounts, and the company wants no servers to manage. Which solution should you recommend?
choices: Azure NetApp Files dual-protocol volumes, because only NetApp Files supports permissions based on Active Directory accounts
Azure Blob Storage with the hierarchical namespace, because POSIX ACLs on directories give the users their existing permissions
Azure File Sync on a new Windows Server VM in Azure, because a server endpoint is needed for SMB shares to use domain permissions
An Azure Files SMB share with identity-based authentication through on-premises AD DS, which keeps the existing permissions
quiz.explain: Azure Files SMB shares support identity-based access with on-premises AD DS and Windows ACLs, with no file server to run. Choice A is tempting because NetApp Files also supports SMB with Active Directory, but it targets demanding low-latency or multiprotocol workloads, and Azure Files supports AD-based permissions too.

days.recap: Use general-purpose v2 accounts with the hierarchical namespace for data lakes, place blobs in hot, cool, cold or archive by how often and how fast they are read, automate tiering with lifecycle rules and lock records with immutability, pick redundancy by the failure to survive, and choose Azure Files, File Sync or NetApp Files by protocol, location and performance.

days.title: Data Integration and Analysis: Data Factory, Microsoft Fabric and Synapse, Databricks, Stream Analytics and Event Hubs Capture

concepts.heading: Azure Data Factory Building Blocks
concepts.body: Azure Data Factory is the managed service for orchestrating data movement and transformation. Pipelines contain activities: the copy activity moves data between more than a hundred connectors with format conversion, mapping data flows run code-free joins, aggregates and cleansing on managed Spark clusters, and external activities hand work to Databricks notebooks, stored procedures or other compute. Integration runtimes provide the compute. The Azure integration runtime is serverless and reaches public endpoints, or private ones when it runs in a managed virtual network with managed private endpoints, which also protects against data exfiltration. The self-hosted integration runtime runs on your own machine to reach data behind a firewall using outbound connections only. The Azure-SSIS integration runtime runs existing SSIS packages with minimal rework. Triggers start pipelines: schedule triggers on a clock, tumbling window triggers for contiguous time slices with backfill, retries and window start and end values, and event triggers when blobs arrive or custom events occur.

concepts.heading: Microsoft Fabric and Azure Synapse Analytics
concepts.body: Microsoft Fabric is a software-as-a-service analytics platform that brings data engineering, data warehousing, data science, real-time analytics and Power BI together on one data lake called OneLake, which stores tables in the open Delta format. Lakehouses and warehouses are items in a workspace rather than separate services to deploy, and capacity is shared across them. Two features remove ETL work: mirroring continuously replicates operational databases such as Azure SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance and Azure Cosmos DB into OneLake, and shortcuts point to data that already sits in Data Lake Storage, Amazon S3 or other OneLake items without copying it. Azure Synapse Analytics remains available, with serverless SQL pools that query lake files in place and bill per data processed, dedicated SQL pools for provisioned warehousing, Spark pools and pipelines. Learn points new analytics projects toward Fabric, so a design for a new unified platform with self-service reporting usually lands there, while existing Synapse estates keep running.

concepts.heading: Azure Databricks
concepts.body: Azure Databricks is a managed analytics platform built on Apache Spark, with Delta Lake, MLflow, Structured Streaming and Unity Catalog integrated. Teams work in collaborative notebooks in Python, SQL, Scala and R, build ETL with Spark and Delta, ingest new files incrementally with Auto Loader, and track machine learning experiments and models with MLflow. Data stays in your own Data Lake Storage as Delta tables in a lakehouse design, and Unity Catalog governs access, lineage and discovery across workspaces. Compute runs as clusters or serverless compute that start for jobs and can scale automatically. Choose Databricks when engineers and data scientists want code-first Spark, notebooks and machine learning on an open lakehouse; choose Data Factory mapping data flows for code-free transformations; and choose Fabric when the priority is one SaaS platform with Power BI built in.

concepts.heading: Azure Stream Analytics
concepts.body: Azure Stream Analytics is a fully managed stream processing service for near-real-time analytics with no clusters to manage. A job reads from inputs such as Event Hubs, IoT Hub or Blob Storage, runs a SQL query with temporal extensions, and writes to outputs such as Azure SQL Database, Cosmos DB, Data Lake Storage, Power BI, Event Hubs or Functions. Windowing functions group events by time: tumbling windows are fixed and do not overlap, hopping windows are fixed but overlap because they hop forward by a smaller period, sliding windows emit output only when the content of the window changes, session windows group events that arrive close together and close after a gap of inactivity, and snapshot windows group events with the same timestamp. Choose Stream Analytics for SQL-based aggregations, filters and alerts on streams; choose Spark Structured Streaming in Databricks when the logic needs code or machine learning.

concepts.heading: Event Hubs and Capture
concepts.body: Azure Event Hubs is a big data streaming platform that ingests millions of events per second through partitions, with consumer groups letting several applications read the same stream independently, and a Kafka-compatible endpoint for existing Kafka clients. Events are kept only for the configured retention period, so the hub is a buffer, not an archive. Event Hubs Capture writes the stream automatically to Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage, per partition in Apache Avro files, whenever a time or size window is reached, with no consumer code to write or run. It needs the Standard tier or higher, because the Basic tier does not support Capture, and its destination must be a non-premium storage account. Capture is the classic cold path of a lambda-style design: Stream Analytics or another consumer handles the hot path in real time, while the captured raw files feed batch processing in Databricks, Synapse or Fabric.

examPoints: A question about copying from a firewalled on-premises source is testing the self-hosted integration runtime; running existing SSIS packages is the Azure-SSIS runtime; locked-down cloud stores without VMs are a managed virtual network with managed private endpoints.

A question about a new unified SaaS analytics platform, mirroring operational databases or querying lake data without copying it points to Microsoft Fabric; code-first Spark with Delta and MLflow points to Databricks; pay-per-query T-SQL over files points to Synapse serverless SQL.

A question about SQL aggregates over a stream is testing Stream Analytics and its window types, and one about keeping every raw event in the lake without code is testing Event Hubs Capture on Standard or higher.

quiz.q: A website streams clickstream events to Event Hubs. Analysts want, in near real time, the number of pages each visitor views per visit, where a visit ends after 10 minutes without any clicks from that visitor. Which approach should you recommend?
choices: A Stream Analytics job that groups events by visitor in tumbling windows of 10 minutes and counts the page views in each window
Event Hubs Capture writing the events to Data Lake Storage every 10 minutes, followed by a nightly batch job that counts visits
A Stream Analytics job that groups events by visitor in hopping windows of 10 minutes that hop forward by one minute each time
A Stream Analytics job that groups events by visitor in session windows with a 10-minute timeout and counts the page views
quiz.explain: A session window groups events that arrive close together and closes after the configured gap of inactivity, which matches a visit that ends after 10 idle minutes. Choice A is tempting because 10 minutes appears in it too, but tumbling windows cut the stream at fixed clock times, so one visit can be split across windows.

quiz.q: A retailer runs separate tools for ingestion, a data warehouse and Power BI reports, and copies the same data between them. It wants one SaaS analytics platform with a single data lake, where reports can also use its Azure SQL Database data without new ETL pipelines. What should you recommend?
choices: Azure Databricks with Unity Catalog, which replaces the warehouse and runs the Power BI reports as Spark notebooks in a workspace
Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pools, loading the Azure SQL data each night with Data Factory copy activities into a warehouse
Microsoft Fabric with OneLake, mirroring the Azure SQL database so that reports query the replicated tables without any ETL work
Azure Stream Analytics with Power BI outputs, which sends every change in the Azure SQL database to the reports as it happens
quiz.explain: Fabric is a SaaS platform with one lake, OneLake, and Power BI built in, and mirroring replicates Azure SQL Database into it continuously without pipelines. Choice B is tempting because Synapse offers warehousing, but nightly copy activities are exactly the ETL the retailer wants to remove, and it is not a single SaaS platform.

days.recap: Orchestrate and copy with Data Factory and the right integration runtime, build new unified analytics on Microsoft Fabric with mirroring and shortcuts, use Databricks for code-first Spark and machine learning, aggregate streams with Stream Analytics windows, and keep raw events in the lake with Event Hubs Capture.

days.title: Backup Design: RPO and RTO, Vaults, Policies, Immutability, and Cross Region Restore

concepts.heading: Start From RPO and RTO
concepts.body: Every continuity design starts with two numbers per workload. The recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data, measured in time, the business can afford to lose; the recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the workload may be down before it runs again. Backup and restore gives an RPO of hours (one or a few backups a day) and an RTO that includes rebuilding disks from the vault, so it suits a reporting server that can lose a day of data and be down for a day. An order system with a five-minute RPO and a two-hour RTO needs replication with Azure Site Recovery or a database replica instead. Backups still matter for every tier, because replication faithfully copies deletions, corruption and encrypted ransomware files, while a backup keeps older recovery points. Group workloads into tiers by their RPO and RTO, then pick the cheapest technique that meets each tier.

concepts.heading: Two Vault Types and What Each Protects
concepts.body: Azure Backup stores recovery points in a vault in the same region as the protected workload. A Recovery Services vault protects Azure VMs, SQL Server and SAP HANA running in Azure VMs, Azure Files, and on-premises machines through the MARS agent (files, folders, system state) or Microsoft Azure Backup Server (app-aware SQL Server, Exchange and Hyper-V). A Backup vault protects newer workloads: Azure Blob Storage (vaulted backup), managed disks through Azure Disk Backup, Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server and AKS clusters. Both types support soft delete, immutability and multiuser authorization, and the policy and monitoring for an item live in the vault of its workload type. In a Recovery Services vault, set storage redundancy, LRS, ZRS or GRS, before you configure the first backup, because the option is then disabled. ZRS keeps backups inside the region across zones for data residency, and GRS also copies them to the paired region.

concepts.heading: Policies That Set Frequency and Retention
concepts.body: A backup policy sets how often backups run and how long daily, weekly, monthly and yearly recovery points are kept, for example daily points for 30 days and yearly points for 10 years. For VMs, the Standard policy takes one backup a day; the Enhanced policy takes several a day, as often as every four hours, keeps instant restore snapshots on zone-redundant storage for up to 30 days, supports Trusted Launch VMs (Standard supports them only through CLI, PowerShell or REST) and is required for Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks. A VM moved to the Enhanced policy cannot go back to Standard. SQL Server in an Azure VM gets a workload backup with full, differential and log backups; log backups as often as every 15 minutes give a 15-minute RPO and per-database point-in-time restore. Azure Disk Backup takes agentless incremental snapshots of managed disks several times a day. For blobs, operational backup stays inside the source account, while vaulted backup copies data to the Backup vault so it survives deletion of the account.

concepts.heading: Protecting the Backups Themselves
concepts.body: Attackers delete backups before they encrypt production, so a design must protect the vault. Soft delete is on by default and keeps deleted backup data for 14 days, extendable up to 180 days, so backups deleted long before an attack is noticed can still be undeleted; deletion itself is still allowed. Immutability blocks operations that could lose recovery points, such as deleting them before they expire or reducing retention, for every item in the vault. Enable it, confirm daily operations still work, then lock it: a locked immutable vault cannot be turned back, not even by a vault administrator. Multiuser authorization adds a Resource Guard, ideally owned by a security team in a different subscription or tenant, so critical operations such as disabling soft delete or shortening retention fail until that team grants access. Use all three together for ransomware resilience: soft delete for recovery, immutability for retention, and a second party for changes.

concepts.heading: Cross Region Restore and Its Limits
concepts.body: A GRS vault replicates backup data to the paired region. Without Cross Region Restore, that secondary copy is used only if Microsoft declares a disaster for the primary region. Enabling Cross Region Restore lets you restore VMs, SQL and other supported items in the secondary region whenever you choose, which also lets you run audited restore drills. The trade-off is time: Learn notes the secondary-region RPO for VM backups can be up to 36 hours in the worst case, because daily vaulting is followed by replication lag, and every disk must be rebuilt from the vault. That is fine for a server that tolerates a day of loss, but it is not a substitute for Site Recovery when the RPO is minutes. For Azure Files, choose the vaulted tier in a Recovery Services vault when backups must survive the loss of the storage account and support cross-region restore; snapshot backups stay in the same account.

examPoints: A question that gives an RPO of minutes and an RTO of hours across regions is testing that backup and restore is too slow and that Site Recovery or a database replica is needed.

A question about ransomware, a compromised backup administrator or backups that must not be deleted before they expire is testing soft delete retention, locked immutability and multiuser authorization with a Resource Guard.
A question that names Trusted Launch, Premium SSD v2, several backups a day, or restores in the paired region on demand is testing the Enhanced VM policy and Cross Region Restore on a GRS vault.

quiz.q: A bank's security policy says a compromised backup administrator account must not be able to shorten retention or disable soft delete in a Recovery Services vault without approval from the security team. Security staff must not run day-to-day backup operations. What should you recommend?
choices: A custom RBAC role for backup administrators that removes the delete permissions on backup items and policies
Multiuser authorization with a Resource Guard that the security team owns in a separate subscription
Cross Region Restore on a GRS vault, so recovery points deleted in one region remain in the paired region
Soft delete extended to 180 days, so that retention changes wait for a security review before they apply
quiz.explain: Multiuser authorization makes protected operations such as reducing retention or disabling soft delete fail until the Resource Guard owner grants access, while backup admins keep running daily jobs. Choice A is tempting, but a custom role does not cover every critical operation, and anyone who can manage roles can restore the permission.

quiz.q: A line-of-business app runs on Trusted Launch VMs with Premium SSD v2 data disks. The business accepts an RPO of four hours and wants VM-level restore points kept for 30 days. Which design meets this?
choices: Azure Site Recovery replication of each VM, with app-consistent snapshots every four hours
A Standard VM backup policy in a Recovery Services vault, with four daily schedules added
The MARS agent inside each VM, with a file and folder backup schedule every four hours
An Enhanced VM backup policy in a Recovery Services vault, scheduled every four hours
quiz.explain: The Enhanced policy supports several backups a day and is required for Premium SSD v2 disks, which the Standard policy cannot protect. Choice A is tempting because Site Recovery replicates often, but it is a disaster recovery tool for failover, not a backup with 30 days of governed recovery points.

days.recap: Size each workload by RPO and RTO, protect VMs, SQL in VMs and Azure Files in a Recovery Services vault and blobs, disks, PostgreSQL and AKS in a Backup vault, guard backups with soft delete, locked immutability and a Resource Guard, and use Cross Region Restore only where hours of RPO are acceptable.

days.title: Disaster Recovery: Site Recovery, Recovery Plans, and Database Restore Options

concepts.heading: What Azure Site Recovery Provides
concepts.body: Azure Site Recovery replicates machines continuously so that, after a disaster, Azure creates VMs from the replicated data in another location. Azure-to-Azure replication copies VMs to a secondary region. Zone-to-zone disaster recovery replicates to another availability zone in the same region, for workloads whose data must stay in the region; it is supported in a listed set of regions. For on-premises VMware VMs and physical servers, the modernized architecture uses a replication appliance on-premises and the Mobility service on each machine; Hyper-V uses the Site Recovery Provider and the Recovery Services agent instead. RPO is typically minutes, and RTO is the time to boot the VMs and run the steps of the plan. Site Recovery is not a backup: corruption and deletions replicate too, and it keeps only a short window of recovery points, so pair it with Azure Backup for long retention.

concepts.heading: Recovery Plans Orchestrate Multi-Tier Failover
concepts.body: A recovery plan gathers replicated machines into groups that fail over as a unit, in order. A classic plan starts the database group first, then the application tier, then the web tier, so each tier finds its dependencies running. Each group can have pre and post actions: Azure Automation runbooks for steps such as updating DNS records, changing a connection string or attaching a load balancer, and manual actions for steps a person must confirm. Recovery plans support test failover, planned or unplanned failover and failback, and they shorten RTO by replacing a long checklist with one orchestrated run. After a failover you commit it, re-protect the VMs so they replicate back toward the original region, and later fail back. A hand-written failover script duplicates what a recovery plan does natively and gives no ordered groups or drills, so on the exam prefer the plan.

concepts.heading: Disaster Recovery Drills
concepts.body: A design that has never been tested is a hope, not a plan. A Site Recovery test failover is a drill that brings up copies of the VMs without data loss or downtime and without affecting ongoing replication or production. Run it into an isolated virtual network that mirrors the production address space and includes test copies of supporting services such as domain controllers and DNS. Never test into the production network while the source VMs are running: two machines with the same identity and IP address would conflict. After validating the app, clean up the test failover to delete the test VMs. Run drills on a regular schedule and after major changes, and record the actual recovery time to compare with the RTO. Azure Migrate uses the same idea for migrations: a test migration into an isolated network before cutover.

concepts.heading: Azure SQL Restore: PITR, LTR, and Geo-Restore
concepts.body: Azure SQL Database and SQL Managed Instance take automated backups. Point-in-time restore (PITR) recovers to any point within the short-term retention period, 7 days by default and configurable from 1 to 35 days (Basic: up to 7), into a new database. Long-term retention (LTR) keeps weekly, monthly or yearly full backups for up to 10 years; a policy such as monthly backups for seven years meets most compliance rules. PITR backups are lost when the logical server is deleted, but LTR backups are not, and they can be restored to a new server. Geo-restore creates a new database in any region from geo-replicated backups, even when the source region is down. Learn calls it the most basic disaster recovery option, suited to relatively small, non-critical databases: it recovers from backups, so RPO and RTO are much longer than with a replica, and the endpoint changes. Choosing locally or zone-redundant backup storage disables geo-restore.

concepts.heading: Restore Options for Other Data Stores
concepts.body: Azure Cosmos DB offers two backup modes. Continuous backup allows self-service point-in-time restore within a retention window of 7, 30 or 35 days, depending on the tier you choose. Periodic backup takes full backups at an interval, every four hours by default with two copies kept, and a restore needs a support request. Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server keeps built-in backups for 7 days by default, up to 35, and geo-redundant backup storage can be chosen only when the server is created; for retention beyond 35 days in isolated storage, protect it with Azure Backup in a Backup vault, for up to 10 years. SQL Server on Azure VMs uses the Azure Backup SQL workload backup for point-in-time restore and an Always On availability group for fast failover. Match each store to the requirement: self-service PITR, long retention, or a replica for minutes of RTO.

examPoints: A question that needs several tiers to start in order with a DNS change, and minimal manual work during failover, is testing a Site Recovery recovery plan with ordered groups and an Automation runbook.
A question about proving disaster recovery without affecting production is testing a test failover into an isolated network, followed by cleanup.
A question about keeping database backups for years, surviving a deleted server, or a cheap regional option for a small database is testing long-term retention versus PITR versus geo-restore.

quiz.q: A three-tier app runs on Azure VMs in West Europe. In a regional outage, the database VM must start before the app VMs, which must start before the web VMs, and a DNS record must be updated automatically. The RPO is 15 minutes. What should you recommend?
choices: Azure Backup with Cross Region Restore, plus a runbook that restores the VMs in order
Site Recovery replication, with an engineer failing over each VM by hand in the right order
Site Recovery replication with a recovery plan of three ordered groups and a DNS runbook
Zone-redundant VM deployment across three zones behind a Standard Load Balancer
quiz.explain: Site Recovery meets a minutes-level RPO, and a recovery plan starts the groups in order and runs the DNS update as a post action. Choice A is tempting because it uses a runbook, but restoring from backups in the paired region gives an RPO of hours, far beyond 15 minutes.

quiz.q: A team accidentally overwrote documents in an Azure Cosmos DB container 20 days ago. Next time they want to restore the container themselves to an exact timestamp within the last four weeks, without opening a support case. What should you recommend?
choices: Continuous backup on the 30-day tier, which allows self-service restore to any point in that window
Periodic backup every four hours with two copies retained, restored through the Azure portal
Continuous backup on the 7-day tier, which allows self-service restore to any point in that window
Multi-region writes across two regions, so the second region keeps the documents as they were
quiz.explain: Continuous backup gives self-service point-in-time restore, and the 30-day tier covers four weeks. Choice C is tempting because it is also self-service continuous backup, but seven days cannot reach a change made 20 days ago.

days.recap: Site Recovery replicates VMs from Azure regions, zones, VMware, physical servers and Hyper-V for minutes of RPO, recovery plans order and automate failover, test failovers run in isolated networks, and Azure SQL uses PITR for weeks, LTR for years and geo-restore as the basic regional fallback.

days.title: High Availability for Compute: Zones, Sets, Scale Sets, App Service, and AKS

concepts.heading: Failure Scopes: Rack, Datacenter, Region
concepts.body: Design high availability against a named failure scope. An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains (separate racks with their own power and network) and update domains (groups rebooted at different times during planned maintenance) inside one datacenter. It protects against a rack failure or host maintenance, not against losing the datacenter, and it is the right tool in a region without availability zones. Availability zones are physically separate groups of datacenters in a region, each with independent power, cooling and networking. A zonal resource is pinned to one zone and never survives that zone's outage; a zone-redundant resource is spread across zones by the platform. So six VMs all in zone 1 behind a zone-redundant load balancer still fail with zone 1. A whole-region outage needs a second region, covered on the next day; zones are the default answer for high availability inside a region.

concepts.heading: Virtual Machine Scale Sets
concepts.body: A scale set manages a group of VMs as one fleet with autoscale. Flexible orchestration is the recommended mode for new scale sets: VMs use the standard VM APIs, the set can spread instances across availability zones and fault domains, and it can mix Spot and on-demand VMs in one set. Because each instance is a normal VM, per-VM features such as Azure Backup and Site Recovery work on them. Uniform orchestration is for large fleets of identical, stateless instances managed only through the scale set. To survive a zone loss, spread the scale set across at least two zones and keep enough capacity that the remaining zones can carry the full load, either by over-provisioning or by autoscale rules that react quickly. Stateless tiers fit scale sets best; keep state in zone-redundant data services so any instance can serve any request.

concepts.heading: Zone-Redundant Entry Points and Disks
concepts.body: A zone-spread fleet needs an entry point that is also zone redundant. A Standard Load Balancer with a zone-redundant frontend, built on a zone-redundant Standard public IP, keeps the same address when one zone fails, and its back end can contain VMs in every zone. Basic Load Balancer and Basic public IPs are retired and support no zones, so never choose them. Application Gateway v2 and Azure Firewall can also be deployed across zones. Disks matter too: a locally redundant managed disk lives in one zone, so a VM that uses it is zonal. Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) disks, available for Premium SSD and Standard SSD, keep copies in three zones, and shared ZRS disks let clustered VMs in different zones fail over the same disk. For LRS disks, Microsoft suggests application-level replication, ZRS snapshots or cross-zone Site Recovery, noting the last does not give zero RPO.

concepts.heading: App Service Zone Redundancy
concepts.body: Azure App Service becomes zone redundant at the plan level. The plan must be Premium v2, Premium v3 or Premium v4 on a scale unit that supports zones (an App Service Environment v3 also supports it), and it must run at least two instances; if you ask for fewer, the platform enforces two and bills for two. Every app in that plan becomes zone redundant: Azure spreads the instances across zones and detects zone failures itself, with no extra setting per app. Microsoft suggests over-provisioning so the remaining zones can carry the full load during an outage. Standard and Basic plans cannot be zone redundant, so scaling out a Standard plan adds instances without zone guarantees. Deployment slots, virtual network integration and autoscale are useful features, but none of them adds zone resilience on its own.

concepts.heading: AKS Zone Resilience
concepts.body: For Azure Kubernetes Service, create node pools that span availability zones so nodes are placed in several zones. Kubernetes then needs to spread the pods: use topology spread constraints or anti-affinity on the zone label so replicas of a deployment do not land in one zone. Stateful workloads need storage that can follow a pod: an Azure Disk on LRS is pinned to its zone, so a pod rescheduled to another zone cannot attach it, while a ZRS disk storage class lets the volume attach in any zone. Azure Files and managed databases are other zone-resilient choices for state. Put a zone-redundant entry point, such as a Standard Load Balancer or Application Gateway v2, in front of the cluster. With zone-spanning node pools, spread pods and ZRS volumes, an AKS workload can keep running through a zone outage without manual action.

examPoints: A question with every VM in one zone, or LRS disks under a zone-spread fleet, is testing that zonal resources fail with their zone and need instances and storage in several zones.
A question about a region without availability zones that still needs protection from rack failures and maintenance is testing availability sets or a Flexible scale set spread across fault domains.
A question that asks App Service or AKS to survive a zone outage is testing the Premium v2 to v4 plan with at least two instances, or zone-spanning node pools with spread pods and ZRS disks.

quiz.q: Six web VMs run in zone 1 of a region, behind a Standard Load Balancer with a zone-redundant frontend. The web tier must keep serving requests if any single zone fails. What should you recommend?
choices: Move the frontend to a zonal public IP in zone 1, so traffic always stays next to the VMs
Put the six VMs into an availability set inside zone 1, so they spread across fault domains
Replace the load balancer with Traffic Manager priority routing between the six VMs
Redeploy the VMs as a Flexible scale set across zones 1, 2 and 3 behind the same frontend
quiz.explain: The load balancer frontend already survives a zone loss, but the VMs are zonal and all sit in zone 1; spreading them across three zones fixes the real single point of failure. Choice B is tempting because availability sets add redundancy, but fault domains are racks inside one datacenter, not separate zones.

quiz.q: A customer portal runs on one instance of a Standard App Service plan. The business now requires the portal to survive the failure of one availability zone in its region, without a second region. What should you recommend?
choices: Scale the Standard plan out to three instances, which the platform spreads across the region's zones
Move to a zone-redundant Premium v3 plan with two or more instances on a zone-capable scale unit
Add a staging deployment slot in another zone and swap it into production during a zone outage
Enable virtual network integration for the app with a zone-redundant subnet in the same region
quiz.explain: Zone redundancy needs a Premium v2, v3 or v4 plan on a scale unit with zones and at least two instances, after which every app in the plan is spread across zones. Choice A is tempting because it adds instances, but a Standard plan gives no zone placement guarantees.

days.recap: Availability sets cover racks and maintenance, zones cover datacenter loss, Flexible scale sets spread VMs across zones behind a zone-redundant Standard Load Balancer with ZRS disks, App Service needs a Premium v2 to v4 plan with two or more instances, and AKS needs zone-spanning pools, spread pods and ZRS volumes.

days.title: High Availability for Data: Azure SQL, Cosmos DB, Storage Redundancy, and Multi-Region Design

concepts.heading: Zone Redundancy for Relational Data
concepts.body: Inside one region, zone redundancy is the first answer for databases. Azure SQL Database supports it on the vCore tiers General Purpose, Business Critical and Hyperscale and on DTU Premium; Basic and Standard cannot be zone redundant. General Purpose keeps data and log files on zone-redundant storage with spare stateless compute in other zones, and it is the budget choice among tiers that support zone redundancy. Microsoft states zone redundancy gives zero committed-data loss when one zone fails. SQL Managed Instance also supports zone redundancy. For SQL Server on Azure VMs, build an Always On availability group with synchronous replicas in different zones, so a zone loss fails over automatically. Site Recovery to another zone is a disaster recovery tool with a non-zero RPO and an orchestrated failover, so it does not replace an availability group when the requirement is automatic, zero-loss failover.

concepts.heading: Active Geo-Replication Versus Failover Groups
concepts.body: For a regional outage, Azure SQL offers two replication features. Active geo-replication works per database: it creates up to four readable secondaries in the same or other regions, useful for offloading reads, and you fail over one database at a time, after which the app must connect to the new endpoint. A failover group fails over a group of databases together, or all databases of a managed instance, and gives read-write and read-only listener endpoints whose names do not change, so the connection string stays the same after failover. The failover policy matters. Customer managed is recommended when the RTO is under an hour or you want to decide when and which group fails over. Microsoft managed fails over all Microsoft-managed groups in a region during a widespread outage, after a grace period that cannot be set below one hour. Replication is asynchronous, so a forced failover can lose the latest transactions.

concepts.heading: Cosmos DB Across Zones and Regions
concepts.body: For a Cosmos DB account in one region, enable zone redundancy to survive a zone outage; adding regions protects against regional outages. With one write region and several read regions, service-managed failover promotes a read region if the write region fails. Multi-region writes let every region accept writes locally and keep accepting them through a regional outage, at the cost of conflicts that a conflict resolution policy, last writer wins by default or a custom procedure, must settle. Consistency sets the cross-region RPO. Strong consistency gives zero data loss across regions but requires a single write region and adds write latency. Bounded staleness limits lag to K versions and T time, but in a multi-region account the minimum is still 100,000 writes or 300 seconds, so it is not zero loss. Session, consistent prefix and eventual allow more lag in exchange for lower latency.

concepts.heading: Storage Redundancy Choices
concepts.body: Azure Storage keeps several copies of data, and the option decides which failures it survives. LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter. ZRS keeps copies across three availability zones, so data stays readable and writable through a zone outage. GRS adds an asynchronous copy in the paired secondary region on top of LRS, and GZRS does the same on top of ZRS. The secondary is not readable unless you choose a read-access option: RA-GRS or RA-GZRS lets apps read from the secondary endpoint during a regional outage without waiting for a failover, while writes still need the account to fail over. So zone resilience means a ZRS-based option, reading during a regional outage means an RA option, and both together means RA-GZRS. Azure Files has no RA options; choose ZRS so a share rides through a zone outage without remounting. Managed disks use LRS or ZRS only.

concepts.heading: Multi-Region Patterns and Region Pairs
concepts.body: Multi-region designs come in three shapes. Active-active runs the workload in two or more regions at once behind a global entry point, giving near-zero downtime when a region fails at the highest cost and complexity, because data must replicate in both directions. Active-passive with a warm spare keeps a scaled-down copy running that scales up during failover; a cold spare keeps only data and templates, which is cheaper but slower. Choose by RTO and budget. Region pairs do not give automatic failover: Microsoft warns that deploying into a pair does not by itself provide high availability or failover, and many newer regions are nonpaired and rely on availability zones. Design replication and failover for every component, paired or not: database, storage, secrets, DNS and the entry point. A single-region workload gets high availability from zone redundancy plus backups, not from geo-replication.

examPoints: A question with several databases that must fail over together with an unchanged connection string, or an RTO under an hour, is testing failover groups, their listeners and the customer managed policy.
A question that asks for zero data loss across Cosmos DB regions or local writes everywhere is testing strong consistency with one write region versus multi-region writes with conflict resolution.

A question that combines zone resilience with reads from another region during an outage is testing RA-GZRS, and a question that assumes a region pair fails over on its own is testing that it does not.

quiz.q: A ledger app stores entries in Azure Cosmos DB with replicas in three regions. If the write region fails, no committed entry may be lost. Higher write latency is acceptable. Which configuration should you recommend?
choices: A single write region with strong consistency, plus read regions in the other two locations
Multi-region writes in all three regions, using the default last writer wins conflict resolution
Session consistency with service-managed failover enabled for the account's write region
Bounded staleness set to its minimum lag values, with one write region and two read regions
quiz.explain: Strong consistency is the level that guarantees zero data loss across regions, and it requires a single write region with higher write latency. Choice D is tempting because it bounds lag, but in a multi-region account the minimum is still 100,000 writes or 300 seconds.

quiz.q: A telemetry archive lives in one storage account. Data must stay readable through a zone outage in the primary region, and analysts must be able to read it from another region during a regional outage without waiting for an account failover. Which redundancy option meets this?
choices: ZRS, because zone-redundant storage also keeps a readable copy in the paired region
GRS, because the secondary region becomes readable as soon as the primary region fails
RA-GZRS, which keeps zone copies in the primary and a read-only secondary endpoint
LRS with object replication to a second account in another datacenter of the same region
quiz.explain: RA-GZRS combines zone-redundant copies in the primary region with a readable secondary endpoint in the other region. Choice B is tempting because it copies data to another region, but without read access the secondary cannot be read until a failover.

days.recap: Use zone redundancy first, failover groups with listeners and a customer managed policy for multi-database regional failover, strong consistency for zero-loss Cosmos DB or multi-region writes for local writes, RA-GZRS for zone plus cross-region reads, and never rely on a region pair to fail over by itself.

days.title: Compute Design: VM Families, Spot, Dedicated Hosts, Virtual Desktop, Containers, Functions, Batch, and VMware

concepts.heading: VM Families and Purchase Options
concepts.body: Choose a VM family by what limits the workload. General purpose D-series balances CPU and memory; memory optimized E-series fits databases and in-memory analytics, with the M-series for the very largest; compute optimized F-series fits CPU-bound web servers and batch jobs; burstable B-series fits low average CPU with short spikes, because credits run out under sustained load. GPU N-series splits into NC and ND for compute such as AI training and NV or NG for visualization and virtual desktops. HB and HX are HPC sizes, and DC and EC confidential VMs protect data in use from the host and hypervisor. Spot VMs use spare capacity and can be evicted at any time, so they fit interruptible, rerunnable work such as rendering or dev/test; the Delete eviction policy avoids disk charges after eviction. Azure Dedicated Host gives a physical server to one customer with maintenance control. For steady 24/7 VMs, combine reservations or savings plans with Azure Hybrid Benefit.

concepts.heading: Azure Virtual Desktop Design
concepts.body: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers Windows desktops and apps from session hosts in host pools. A pooled host pool lets many users share multi-session hosts, the low-cost choice for task workers who use the same apps. A personal host pool gives each user a dedicated VM, needed for persistent desktops or users who install software as administrators; Start VM on Connect and autoscale keep those VMs from running while idle. User profiles should live in FSLogix profile containers on Azure Files or Azure NetApp Files in the same region as the session hosts, so any pooled host can load a user's profile quickly. GPU-accelerated desktops for design or engineering apps point to the NV or NG families. Size the pool for peak concurrent users, and use scaling plans to shut down hosts outside working hours.

concepts.heading: Containers: AKS, Container Apps, Container Instances, App Service
concepts.body: Azure Kubernetes Service gives you a managed control plane and the full Kubernetes API, so choose it when you need custom resource definitions, operators, specific node pools or direct control of the cluster, and accept that you plan upgrades and node operations. Azure Container Apps runs on Kubernetes but hides its API: it gives serverless containers with event-driven KEDA scaling, including scale to zero, HTTP ingress, revisions for traffic splitting and Dapr, and Container Apps jobs for finite or scheduled work. Azure Container Instances runs a single container group on demand with Hyper-V isolation, but has no built-in scaling, load balancing or service discovery, so it is a building block for short tasks or bursts. App Service runs web apps and APIs from code or containers with deployment slots and autoscale, and an App Service Environment v3 gives a single-tenant, network-isolated deployment.

concepts.heading: Azure Functions Hosting Plans
concepts.body: Azure Functions runs event-driven code, and the hosting plan sets scaling, networking and cold start. Flex Consumption is the plan Learn recommends for new serverless apps: pay as you go, fast event-driven scale up to 1,000 instances, virtual network integration, memory size choices and optional always-ready instances that reduce cold starts. The legacy Consumption plan has no virtual network integration, and its Linux option is retiring. Both Flex Consumption and Consumption are code-only. The Premium plan keeps prewarmed instances so there is no cold start, supports virtual network integration and runs custom Linux containers, at the cost of always-on capacity. A Dedicated plan runs functions on an App Service plan you already pay for. Pick Flex Consumption for new serverless code that must reach private endpoints, and Premium when a custom container or no cold start is required.

concepts.heading: Azure Batch and Azure VMware Solution
concepts.body: Azure Batch creates and manages pools of compute nodes, installs applications and schedules jobs, so there is no cluster or scheduler software to run yourself. It fits embarrassingly parallel tasks such as rendering frames or running simulations, and tightly coupled MPI jobs on HPC sizes such as the HB family; pools can use Spot nodes for interruptible tasks, and Batch requeues a preempted node's running task on another node. Azure VMware Solution provides private clouds of VMware vSphere clusters on dedicated bare-metal Azure hosts, managed through vCenter. VMware HCX, included at no extra cost, migrates VMs, including vMotion-based methods, and extends networks so VMs keep their IP addresses. Choose it to leave a datacenter quickly while keeping VMware tools and skills; convert to native Azure VMs later only if you want to leave VMware.

examPoints: A question that describes the workload's bottleneck, interruptions, isolation or data-in-use protection is testing the VM family, Spot, Dedicated Host or confidential VM choice.
A question that asks for the Kubernetes API or CRDs, event-driven containers without cluster management, or a one-off container is testing AKS versus Container Apps versus Container Instances.
A question about serverless functions that must reach a virtual network, run a custom container or avoid cold starts is testing Flex Consumption versus Premium.

quiz.q: A studio renders 20,000 independent frames each night. Any frame can be rerun if interrupted, results are needed by morning, and the team wants the lowest cost without running its own scheduler. What should you recommend?
choices: Azure Dedicated Host with D-series VMs that process the frames one after another through the night
An AKS cluster with an on-demand GPU node pool that stays running all day to keep the queue warm
An Azure Batch pool that uses Spot nodes, with Batch requeuing the tasks of any evicted node
One Azure Container Instances container group that renders all of the frames in a single sequence
quiz.explain: Batch schedules thousands of parallel tasks on a managed pool, and Spot nodes cut cost for interruptible, rerunnable work. Choice B is tempting because AKS can run batch jobs, but the team would run a cluster and on-demand nodes all day, which is neither lowest cost nor scheduler-free.

quiz.q: A team builds microservices that must scale to zero when their queue is empty, expose HTTP ingress, and split traffic between revisions. They do not want to manage cluster upgrades or use the Kubernetes API. Which service should you recommend?
choices: Azure Kubernetes Service with KEDA and the cluster autoscaler enabled on a user node pool
Azure Container Apps, with KEDA scale rules on the queue and revision traffic splitting
Azure Container Instances container groups behind an Application Gateway for HTTP routing
An App Service Premium v3 plan with autoscale rules based on the length of the queue
quiz.explain: Container Apps provides event-driven scaling to zero, ingress and revisions without exposing or requiring management of a Kubernetes cluster. Choice A is tempting because it uses the same KEDA scaler, but AKS means operating the cluster and its upgrades, which the team wants to avoid.

days.recap: Match VM families to the bottleneck, Spot to interruptible work and Dedicated Host to physical isolation, pooled or personal host pools to the desktop need, AKS to the Kubernetes API, Container Apps to serverless containers, Flex Consumption or Premium to the function's network and cold-start needs, Batch to parallel jobs and Azure VMware Solution to a fast VMware exit.

days.title: Messaging and Events: Service Bus, Event Grid, Event Hubs, and Storage Queues

concepts.heading: Messages, Discrete Events, and Event Streams
concepts.body: Start by asking what the sender expects. A message carries data that the sender expects someone to process, such as an order or a command; the sender cares that it is handled exactly as intended. An event is a lightweight notification that something happened, such as a blob being created; the publisher has no expectation about what consumers do with it. Discrete events are handled one at a time, while an event stream is a continuous, high-volume series of events, such as telemetry, that is analysed over time. Learn's comparison maps these onto three services: Service Bus for high-value enterprise messages, Event Grid for reacting to discrete events, and Event Hubs for big data streaming. Many solutions use several of them together: Event Grid tells a function that a file arrived, the function sends an order message to Service Bus, and devices stream telemetry into Event Hubs.

concepts.heading: Azure Service Bus
concepts.body: Service Bus is a fully managed enterprise message broker with queues for point-to-point work and topics with subscriptions for publish-subscribe. Subscriptions use filters, SQL or correlation, so each consumer receives only the messages it wants, and new consumers can be added without changing the publisher. Sessions give ordered, first-in-first-out handling per key, such as per customer, and duplicate detection drops a resent message with the same message ID within a time window. Service Bus also offers transactions, scheduled delivery and a dead-letter queue for messages that cannot be processed. The Standard tier is shared and multitenant, with messages up to 256 KB and variable latency. Premium gives dedicated messaging units with predictable performance, messages up to 100 MB, virtual network integration, Private Link and geo-replication. A Service Bus queue is capped at 80 GB, so it is not the place for a huge, featureless backlog.

concepts.heading: Azure Event Grid
concepts.body: Event Grid is a push-based event routing service. System topics publish events from Azure services, such as Blob Storage, resource groups or Key Vault; custom topics publish events from your own apps. Each event subscription filters events by type or subject and pushes them to a handler such as Azure Functions, Logic Apps, a webhook, a Service Bus queue, a Storage queue or Event Hubs, so one source can fan out to several independent handlers without polling. When a handler fails, Event Grid retries with exponential backoff for a limited time and number of attempts, then drops the event unless a dead-letter destination is set. Configure a dead-letter blob container on each important subscription so expired events are kept for reprocessing. Choose Event Grid when the requirement says react to a state change, near real time, with no polling and loose coupling between source and handlers.

concepts.heading: Azure Event Hubs
concepts.body: Event Hubs is a big data streaming platform for millions of events per second from devices, apps and logs. An event hub is divided into partitions for parallel throughput, and events with the same partition key stay ordered within a partition. Consumers read through consumer groups: each independent reader, such as a real-time dashboard and an archive job, uses its own consumer group and tracks its own position, and how far back it can replay is set by the retention period. Event Hubs Capture writes the stream automatically to Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage for batch analysis. Event Hubs also exposes a Kafka endpoint, so existing Kafka producers and consumers can connect by changing configuration rather than code, with no Kafka cluster to run. Choose Event Hubs for telemetry and logs at high volume, not for business messages that need per-message settlement or dead-lettering.

concepts.heading: Storage Queues and Messaging Patterns
concepts.body: Azure Queue Storage offers simple queues inside a storage account. A queue can hold a very large backlog beyond Service Bus limits, messages are up to 64 KB, and storage logs can record every operation, but there are no sessions, topics, duplicate detection or transactions. Choose it for a large, simple work backlog at low cost. Several design patterns appear in scenarios. Queue-based load leveling buffers short write peaks in a queue so a backend drains them at a steady rate when some delay is acceptable. Competing consumers lets several workers read from one queue to scale processing. Claim check stores a large payload in Blob Storage and sends only a reference in the message, which keeps messages small and the broker fast. Publish-subscribe uses Service Bus topics or Event Grid to deliver one message to many consumers. Make consumers idempotent, because brokers deliver at least once.

examPoints: A question about ordered processing per key, duplicate suppression, transactions or filtered subscribers is testing Service Bus queues and topics, with Premium for large messages and Private Link.
A question that reacts to an Azure resource change with several handlers and no polling, or loses events while a handler is down, is testing Event Grid subscriptions and dead-lettering.
A question about high-volume telemetry, several independent readers, replay or existing Kafka clients is testing Event Hubs partitions, consumer groups, retention and the Kafka endpoint.

quiz.q: An insurer's claim app attaches video evidence of up to 300 MB to each claim. Downstream services must process the steps of each claim in order, and the broker must stay fast. What should you recommend?
choices: Send each video inside a Service Bus Premium message, since the Premium tier accepts large messages
Store each video in Blob Storage and send its URL in a Service Bus message with a session per claim
Stream each video through an Event Hubs partition keyed on the claim ID, with Capture enabled
Split each video into 64 KB pieces and enqueue them in order on a Storage queue per claim
quiz.explain: The claim check pattern keeps the payload in Blob Storage and sends only a reference, and Service Bus sessions keyed on the claim ID keep each claim's steps in order. Choice A is tempting because Premium supports large messages, but its 100 MB limit is below 300 MB and pushing large payloads through the broker slows it.

quiz.q: An Event Grid subscription pushes storage events to a partner webhook. During a day-long outage of the webhook, events were lost. Events must be kept for later processing in future outages. What should you recommend?
choices: Raise the maximum delivery attempts on the subscription, so that retries continue until it recovers
Change the source to Event Hubs, so that Event Grid keeps the events for the hub's retention period
Add a second webhook endpoint to the same subscription, so that one of the two always receives them
Configure a dead-letter blob container on the event subscription and reprocess the stored events
quiz.explain: Events that exhaust their retries are written to the dead-letter container instead of being dropped, so they can be reprocessed after the outage. Choice A is tempting, but retries are bounded by a maximum number of attempts and a time to live, so a long outage still ends in dropped events.

days.recap: Service Bus carries ordered, de-duplicated business messages through queues and filtered topics, Event Grid pushes discrete events to many handlers with dead-lettering, Event Hubs ingests streams with partitions, consumer groups, replay and a Kafka endpoint, and Storage queues hold large simple backlogs, with claim check for big payloads.

days.title: APIs, Caching, Configuration, and Deployment Automation

concepts.heading: API Management Tiers and the Self-Hosted Gateway
concepts.body: API Management puts a gateway, a management plane and a developer portal in front of your APIs. Tiers decide networking and scale. Consumption is serverless and billed per call, with no virtual network options, no developer portal, no built-in cache, no self-hosted gateway and no per-key rate limiting. Developer is for non-production only and has no SLA. Among the v2 tiers, Basic v2 cannot reach backends isolated in a virtual network, Standard v2 adds virtual network integration so a public gateway can call private backends, and Premium v2 adds virtual network injection for full isolation and availability zones, but not multi-region deployment. The classic Premium tier is the one that runs gateways in several Azure regions from one instance. The self-hosted gateway, available in Developer and classic Premium (not v2), is a container you run on Docker, Kubernetes or Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes next to APIs on-premises or in other clouds, so traffic stays local while Azure manages the APIs.

concepts.heading: API Management Policies
concepts.body: Policies are XML statements that run in the inbound, backend, outbound and on-error sections of a request. Throttling has two styles: rate-limit and quota count calls per subscription, while rate-limit-by-key and quota-by-key count per a key you choose, such as the user ID from a token or the client IP address, so one noisy caller cannot exhaust a shared subscription. The validate-jwt policy checks tokens from Microsoft Entra ID before a call reaches the backend. Response caching uses cache-lookup and cache-store; the built-in cache is not available in Consumption, where you attach an external Redis-compatible cache and the same policies use it. Other policies rewrite URLs, transform payloads, set headers or return mock responses. Group APIs into products with subscription keys to control which consumers can call which APIs, and keep backend secrets in named values backed by Key Vault.

concepts.heading: Caching with Azure Managed Redis
concepts.body: A cache keeps hot data in memory to cut latency and database load. Learn's retirement FAQ states that Azure Cache for Redis Basic, Standard and Premium retire on 30 September 2028 and Enterprise and Enterprise Flash on 31 March 2027, and Microsoft recommends Azure Managed Redis for new and migrated caches. Azure Managed Redis is built on Redis Enterprise, is zone redundant by default where the region has zones, supports Redis modules, and offers active geo-replication, so instances in several regions can each read and write locally. Its tiers trade memory against compute, and Flash Optimized keeps a small hot set in memory with colder keys on flash for very large caches. The usual pattern is cache-aside: read the cache first, load from the database on a miss and store the result with an expiration; invalidate the entry when the data changes. The database stays the source of truth.

concepts.heading: App Configuration and Key Vault References
concepts.body: Azure App Configuration stores application settings centrally, with labels for environments and feature flags for turning features on without redeploying. A targeting filter releases a flag to named users, groups or a percentage of users, which fits gradual or beta rollouts. Geo-replication adds replicas in other regions for latency and outage resilience, but it is not available in the Free and Developer tiers. Secrets do not belong in App Configuration values. Keep them in Azure Key Vault and store a Key Vault reference in App Configuration; the app's identity resolves the secret from Key Vault at runtime. App Service and Functions also support Key Vault references directly in app settings, resolved through the app's managed identity, so a rotated secret is picked up without a code change. The design rule: App Configuration for settings and flags, Key Vault for secrets, keys and certificates, and managed identities to read both.

concepts.heading: Infrastructure as Code and Safe Releases
concepts.body: Bicep is the declarative language for Azure Resource Manager deployments, with modules for reuse and what-if to preview changes. A deployment stack manages the resources a template deploys as one unit across resource groups or a subscription. Its actionOnUnmanage setting decides whether resources removed from the template are detached or deleted, and deny settings can block deletes, or writes and deletes, by anyone outside the stack, even subscription owners. Deployment stacks and template specs are the successors to Azure Blueprints, which is retiring. GitHub Actions can deploy without stored secrets through OpenID Connect: a federated credential on a Microsoft Entra app or managed identity, scoped to a repository, branch or environment, plus azure/login with id-token write permission. On App Service, deployment slots let you deploy to staging, warm it up and swap; slot settings stay with their slot, swap with preview validates production settings first, and swapping back is the rollback.

examPoints: A question that needs APIs to stay local on-premises or in another cloud, private backends from a public gateway, or several Azure regions from one instance is testing the self-hosted gateway, Standard v2 integration and classic Premium.
A question about central settings, gradual feature rollout or secrets for many apps is testing App Configuration with feature flags and Key Vault references, not secrets stored as plain settings.
A question about removing resources dropped from a template, blocking deletion outside the pipeline or deploying without secrets is testing deployment stacks and OIDC federated credentials.

quiz.q: A platform team deploys landing zone networking with a pipeline. Resources removed from the template must be deleted on the next run, and nobody outside the pipeline, including subscription Contributors, may delete the deployed resources. What should you recommend?
choices: An Azure Blueprints assignment that uses the Locked resource locking mode for the networking
A Bicep deployment in complete mode at resource group scope, run by the same pipeline each time
A template spec shared through RBAC, with a CanNotDelete lock added on each resource group
A deployment stack with deny settings that block deletion and unmanaged resources set to delete
quiz.explain: A deployment stack tracks every resource it deployed, deletes resources dropped from the template when actionOnUnmanage is set to delete, and its deny settings block deletes outside the stack. Choice A is tempting because Blueprints once did this, but Blueprints is retiring and deployment stacks are its successor.

quiz.q: Twelve App Service apps share common settings. Operations wants to release a new checkout feature to a group of beta users without redeploying, and database passwords must stay in Key Vault. What should you recommend?
choices: App Configuration with a feature flag and targeting filter, plus Key Vault references for passwords
App settings on each app, with deployment slot settings holding the values for the beta users
App Configuration key-values for all settings and passwords, encrypted with a customer-managed key
Key Vault secrets for every setting and feature flag, read by each app once when it starts
quiz.explain: App Configuration centralizes settings and its targeting filter releases a flag to chosen users without a redeploy, while Key Vault references keep passwords in Key Vault. Choice C is tempting because it centralizes everything, but secrets belong in Key Vault, not as App Configuration values.

days.recap: Pick the API Management tier by networking, regions and billing, use self-hosted gateways for local traffic and keyed policies for per-caller limits, cache with Azure Managed Redis and cache-aside, keep settings and flags in App Configuration and secrets in Key Vault, and deploy with Bicep, deployment stacks, OIDC and slots.

days.title: Migrations: Cloud Adoption Framework, Azure Migrate, Databases, and Unstructured Data

concepts.heading: Cloud Adoption Framework and Migration Strategies
concepts.body: The Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) guides adoption through Strategy, Plan, Ready and Adopt, with Govern, Secure and Manage running alongside. Strategy sets business goals, Plan inventories workloads and chooses an approach for each, Ready builds the landing zone (identity, networking, governance and management foundations), and Adopt migrates and modernizes. For each workload CAF lists strategies: Retire workloads with limited business value or where migration costs outweigh the benefits; Retain those that must stay put for now; Rehost a stable, Azure-compatible workload with minimal change when the deadline matters; Replatform to PaaS with minimal code changes to offload maintenance, such as moving an app from VMs to App Service; Refactor code to reduce technical debt; Rearchitect for cloud-native capabilities; Rebuild from scratch; and Replace with a SaaS or AI solution when little customization is needed. Exam stems usually hide the strategy in the business driver.

concepts.heading: Azure Migrate Discovery, Dependencies, and Assessments
concepts.body: Azure Migrate is the hub for discovery, assessment and migration. The Azure Migrate appliance discovers VMware, Hyper-V and physical servers agentlessly and keeps sending configuration and performance data; importing a CSV is a quick, static alternative without performance history. Agentless dependency analysis maps the connections between servers, so you can group servers that must migrate together and build application assessments from the map. Assessments recommend Azure targets, such as Azure VMs, Azure VMware Solution, Azure SQL or App Service, and estimate cost. Performance-based sizing right-sizes oversized on-premises servers from collected data, while as-on-premises sizing copies the current size; add a comfort factor for seasonal peaks or short performance history. A business case answers whether to migrate and what it saves, with total cost of ownership, cash flows and the move from capital to operational expense. Azure Hybrid Benefit and uptime assumptions change cost, not size.

concepts.heading: Migrating Servers and Apps
concepts.body: Azure Migrate migration follows replicate, test, cut over. Replication copies the source VMs to Azure continuously. A test migration starts copies in an isolated virtual network so the team can validate the app without touching the source VMs or production traffic, and it can be repeated. At cutover you stop the source, run a final sync and start the Azure VMs, then update DNS and clients. Build the landing zone first so migrated servers land in governed subscriptions with networking, identity and monitoring in place. Not every server should become a VM: a web app that only needs patching relief can replatform to App Service, and Azure Migrate can assess web apps for App Service or AKS. When a whole VMware estate must leave a datacenter quickly with its tools and IP addresses, Azure VMware Solution with HCX avoids converting each VM.

concepts.heading: Migrating Databases
concepts.body: Choose a database path by target and allowed downtime. In an offline migration, downtime starts when the migration starts; an online migration keeps syncing until a short cutover. Microsoft recommends testing an offline run first and moving to online if its downtime is too long. Azure Database Migration Service supports SQL Server to Azure SQL Database offline only, so minimal downtime into Azure SQL Database uses transactional replication. Into SQL Managed Instance, which keeps instance features such as SQL Agent and cross-database queries, you have three online paths: DMS online, the Log Replay Service in continuous mode, which restores full, differential and log backups from Blob Storage while the databases stay in a restoring state until cutover, and the Managed Instance link, which replicates near real time through a distributed availability group and gives a readable copy for months before it becomes the migration. MySQL uses DMS online and PostgreSQL the built-in migration service online for flexible server.

concepts.heading: Moving Unstructured Data
concepts.body: Start with the arithmetic: 400 TB over a 200 Mbps link takes about six months, so the network cannot carry it in time. AzCopy is a command-line tool for scripted one-off or incremental copies of small to medium size, typically under 1 TB per job, from local files, other storage accounts, Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage. Azure Storage Mover is a managed migration service for larger moves, typically above 1 TB or millions of files, from SMB and NFS shares, with agents near the source and jobs tracked centrally from one storage mover resource. Azure Data Box is a rugged device Microsoft ships to you for offline transfer when bandwidth is the problem; current next-generation devices hold 120 TB or 525 TB of usable capacity, and Data Box Heavy is retired. A common design seeds the bulk with Data Box, then runs Storage Mover jobs to copy changes made since the snapshot, and a final job at cutover.

examPoints: A question that gives a business driver such as a deadline, patching relief, low value or an available SaaS product is testing the CAF strategy, and one about migration readiness is testing the landing zone in Ready.
A question about which servers move together, sizing oversized servers or proving savings is testing dependency analysis, performance-based assessments and the business case.

A question about minimal downtime into Azure SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, MySQL or PostgreSQL, or about bandwidth versus data volume, is testing the database migration path and AzCopy versus Storage Mover versus Data Box.

quiz.q: A company licensed a SaaS HR suite last year. Its old on-premises HR app is still used by a few staff, has had no development for years, and the SaaS suite already covers its functions with little customization needed. Which CAF migration strategy fits the old app?
choices: Replace, moving its users to the SaaS suite so no internal team has to run the application
Rehost, moving the app's servers to Azure VMs unchanged so the staff keep using the same app
Retain, keeping the app on-premises until the datacenter lease ends and then reassessing it
Refactor, changing the app's code to use Azure SDKs so it runs efficiently on Azure services
quiz.explain: CAF's Replace strategy covers moving to a SaaS solution that simplifies operations when little customization is needed, which is exactly what the licensed suite offers. Choice B is tempting because rehosting is quick, but it keeps running and paying for an app whose functions are already covered.

quiz.q: A research lab must move 40 TB of files from an on-premises NAS to Azure Blob Storage over a 10 Gbps ExpressRoute circuit. Leadership wants the migration tracked centrally without custom scripts, and changed files must be copied again before cutover. What should you recommend?
choices: Azure Data Box shipments, because any transfer larger than 10 TB has to travel offline on a device
AzCopy run from an administrator's workstation as a scheduled task every night until cutover
Azure Storage Mover with an agent near the NAS and migration jobs rerun for the changed files
Azure Migrate server migration of the NAS appliance, replicated as a VM into the target region
quiz.explain: At 10 Gbps, 40 TB moves in well under a day, and Storage Mover gives managed, centrally tracked jobs that can be rerun to copy changes. Choice A is tempting because the data set is large, but Data Box is for links that cannot carry the data in time, and no size rule forces it.

days.recap: Use CAF from Strategy to Adopt with a landing zone first, pick one of the eight strategies from the business driver, discover with the Azure Migrate appliance, group by dependencies, test before cutover, choose online database paths by target, and match AzCopy, Storage Mover or Data Box to data volume and bandwidth.

days.title: Connectivity: Internet Egress, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, Virtual WAN, and Hub-Spoke

concepts.heading: Internet Connectivity and Outbound Design
concepts.body: Public IP addresses use the Standard SKU, which is secure by default, supports zones and can be zone redundant; Basic SKU public IPs are retired and never a design answer. Inbound traffic should arrive through a load balancer, Application Gateway, Azure Firewall or Front Door rather than a public IP on every VM. Outbound traffic from a private IP uses source network address translation (SNAT), and each connection to the same destination needs its own source port on the public IP. Outbound rules on a Standard Load Balancer pre-allocate a limited number of ports per instance, which can run out under load and also expose an inbound frontend. Azure NAT Gateway, attached to a subnet, gives all its VMs predictable outbound addresses from public IPs or a public IP prefix, allocates SNAT ports dynamically across the subnet to minimize exhaustion, and allows no inbound connections. Partners that allowlist a fixed IP range are a classic NAT Gateway clue.

concepts.heading: VPN Gateway
concepts.body: Azure VPN Gateway sends encrypted IPsec traffic over the internet. Site-to-site connects on-premises networks, point-to-site connects individual users, and VNet-to-VNet connects virtual networks. It is quick to set up and costs less than a private circuit, but bandwidth and latency depend on the internet path. For resilience, choose a zone-redundant gateway SKU so the gateway instances run in different zones, and use active-active mode, with tunnels from each on-premises device to both gateway instances, so one instance or one device can fail without an outage. Use BGP for dynamic routing between sites. The Basic VPN SKU supports neither active-active nor zone redundancy, and has no BGP, so it does not fit production designs. A VPN gateway can also coexist with an ExpressRoute gateway in the same virtual network to provide an encrypted backup path.

concepts.heading: ExpressRoute, Premium, Global Reach, and FastPath
concepts.body: ExpressRoute is a private connection from on-premises to Microsoft through a connectivity provider at a peering location, so traffic does not cross the public internet. Private peering reaches virtual networks; Microsoft peering reaches Microsoft public services. The Premium add-on gives global connectivity to Azure regions in other geopolitical regions and raises the route limit on private peering from 4,000 to 10,000. Global Reach links two circuits so on-premises sites exchange traffic over Microsoft's backbone; across geopolitical regions both circuits need Premium.
